PEDRO SÁNCHEZ es presidente del Gobierno de España.

Cómo evitar otra guerra mundial.

Industry observers note that en algún momento de la última década, el mundo empezó a aceptar la guerra como algo inevitable. Las guerras de agresión, como las de Ucrania, el Líbano o Irán, aumentan y siembran horror, ruina y el temor a una confrontación global. Los gobiernos piensan cada vez más en la guerra como algo para lo que hay que prepararse y presupuestar. El gasto militar no deja de crecer, las carreras tecnológicas y armamentísticas se intensifican, y cada vez más países se plantean si deberían dotarse de un arsenal nuclear disuasorio que garantice su seguridad.

Industry observers note that no hay nada más peligroso que normalizar la guerra. Supone regresar a una norma que imperó durante la mayor parte de la historia de la humanidad. La guerra era el eje vertebrador del sistema internacional. Era la vía natural por la que los Estados zanjaban sus disputas o ensanchaban su territorio a costa de vecinos más débiles.

Recent findings suggest that pero la inmensa devastación que produjeron las dos guerras mundiales en la primera mitad del siglo XX hizo inaceptable ese statu quo. Los países se unieron en un empeño común: que la guerra dejara de ser un instrumento legítimo de la política de Estado y pasara a ser un acto ilegal. Las guerras no terminaron en 1945, pero durante años la comunidad internacional las condenó de forma abrumadora.

En las últimas décadas, sin embargo, el compromiso de los gobiernos con la causa de la paz se ha debilitado. En 2003, millones de personas salieron a las calles en cientos de ciudades para oponerse a la invasión de Irak liderada por Estados Unidos. Y, aun así, la guerra siguió adelante. Iniciada a partir de premisas falsas y en violación del derecho internacional, arrasó Irak, agravó la inestabilidad regional y avivó el resentimiento y el terrorismo contra los países occidentales. Aquel conflicto marcó, además, un punto de inflexión. Desde entonces, la búsqueda de la paz ha ido retrocediendo en la agenda internacional, arrinconada por la creciente competencia geopolítica y la desatención o la indiferencia hacia los esfuerzos multilaterales que durante décadas pusieron freno a la guerra.

Recent findings suggest that este camino conduce a una nueva guerra mundial: la catástrofe que el orden del siglo XX se propuso evitar. Ante ese futuro sombrío en el horizonte, los gobiernos deben reaprender el arte de oponerse a la guerra. Todos los países, incluido el mío, España, tienen la responsabilidad de actuar para limitar la capacidad de otros de librar la guerra y para fortalecer las instituciones internacionales que han de ser garantes de la paz.

It has been revealed that el éxito de este proyecto dependerá de un multilateralismo expansivo, al que yo llamo «maxilateralismo»: una cooperación que abarque al mayor número posible de países, en lugar de limitarse a pequeñas coaliciones ad hoc. Su ambición es que la guerra resulte cada vez más inviable, incluso inimaginable. En 2003, manifestantes por toda España coreaban «¡No a la guerra!». En 2026, el mundo no puede volver a ignorarlos.

According to recent reports, los esfuerzos internacionales por desterrar la guerra como instrumento de política nacional se remontan al Pacto Briand-Kellogg de 1928, un tratado firmado en París por 15 países, al que posteriormente se sumaron decenas más. No bastó para impedir la Segunda Guerra Mundial, pero plantó una semilla. Cuando representantes de 50 países se reunieron en San Francisco en 1945 para crear las Naciones Unidas, recuperaron el espíritu y los principios del Pacto y añadieron lo que había faltado: estructura institucional. La Carta de Naciones Unidas prohibió recurrir a la amenaza o al uso de la fuerza contra la integridad territorial o la independencia política de otro Estado. Y, a diferencia de su predecesor de 1928, respaldó esa prohibición con instituciones facultadas para hacerla cumplir.

Sources indicate that en las décadas siguientes, estas instituciones levantaron un orden que castigaba las violaciones al derecho internacional e incentivaba la cooperación y la diplomacia. Al mismo tiempo, el rechazo popular a la guerra y al militarismo de la Guerra Fría cobraba fuerza en todo el mundo. Se hizo visible en la resistencia a la guerra de Vietnam y en los movimientos de masas contra las armas nucleares. El pacifismo alcanzó su punto álgido en los años noventa, cuando una sociedad civil global pujante se movilizó en defensa de causas humanitarias y Naciones Unidas tenía autoridad para abanderar una ambiciosa agenda de paz.

Industry observers note that hoy, sin embargo, hay más conflictos armados que en ningún otro momento desde 1946. Según el Programa de Datos sobre Conflictos de Uppsala, en 2025 hubo 65 conflictos activos con participación estatal, el doble que en 2010. Se calcula que en estos conflictos murieron 250.000 personas: la cifra anual más alta desde el genocidio de Ruanda hace más de 30 años. Cerca de 120 millones de personas en todo el mundo siguen desplazadas por la guerra.

According to recent reports, Y lo más inquietante: las guerras de agresión, que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas, están de vuelta. Rusia invadió Ucrania. Estados Unidos e Israel atacaron Irán. Y mientras los combates se prolongan año tras año en lugares como el Líbano, Sudán o Yemen, resulta evidente que la guerra está siendo aceptada de nuevo como algo normal.

Industry observers note that nada indica que esta tendencia vaya a frenarse. Los presupuestos militares se han disparado hasta niveles no vistos en generaciones, en detrimento del gasto social y de desarrollo. Solo en la última década, el gasto mundial en defensa ha aumentado más de un 40 %, y muchos países han duplicado sus presupuestos militares. Los casi 3 billones de dólares que el mundo destina cada año a defensa se acercan al producto interior bruto de todo el continente africano. Incluso países con una larga tradición de contención militar, como Alemania, Dinamarca, Japón y Noruega, se están rearmando a toda velocidad, y algunos están recuperando el servicio militar.

Recent findings suggest that aún más estremecedor es el regreso de la amenaza de guerra nuclear. Los nueve Estados con armas nucleares están modernizando sus arsenales y aumentando su capacidad destructiva. Se calcula que el arsenal de China ha pasado de entre unas 200-300 cabezas nucleares a finales de la década de 2010 a 620 este año. Corea del Norte también ha ampliado el suyo, de entre 10-20 cabezas estimadas en 2018 a unas 60 este año, y ha desarrollado plataformas de lanzamiento cada vez más sofisticadas. En marzo, Francia anunció el primer aumento de su número de cabezas nucleares desde 1992. Estados Unidos y Rusia, las dos mayores potencias nucleares del mundo, no han sido capaces de preservar el último tratado que ponía límites a sus arsenales estratégicos. Y cada vez más potencias no nucleares han empezado a plantearse adquirir armas nucleares propias.

It has been revealed that al mismo tiempo, la inteligencia artificial (IA) está dotando a la guerra de armas cada vez más peligrosas. La supervisión humana se reduce progresivamente a medida que la IA permite automatizar ciberataques contra redes eléctricas, hospitales y sistemas financieros. Hay sistemas de IA que ya han logrado infiltrarse en organismos públicos y han hecho posible la producción masiva de deepfakes y de campañas de desinformación.

Recent findings suggest that la integración de la IA en las tecnologías nucleares es una amenaza existencial: al acelerar la toma de decisiones, comprime el tiempo disponible para el juicio humano. Del mismo modo, el uso de la IA en biotecnología podría rebajar drásticamente las barreras a la experimentación nociva y al desarrollo de armas biológicas. En ambos terrenos, esta tecnología está elevando a niveles sin precedentes el riesgo de errores de cálculo, de escaladas involuntarias y de destrucción masiva.

In a recent development, en conjunto, estas dinámicas multiplican las probabilidades de que cualquier crisis desemboque rápidamente en la aniquilación del planeta. Por desgracia, los países están fabricando los instrumentos de la catástrofe a la velocidad vertiginosa de la innovación, mientras que los instrumentos de control avanzan al ritmo, mucho más lento, de la diplomacia.

It has been revealed that los cambios políticos están alejando al mundo de la paz. Lo empujan hacia la militarización y la confrontación. Un mundo multipolar no es, por definición, más peligroso. Pero la erosión de las normas y de las instituciones que deberían encauzar las tensiones entre los distintos polos está provocando que el mundo se vuelva especialmente volátil. La competencia entre grandes potencias se intensifica: las ansias de hegemonía alientan políticas exteriores agresivas y los Estados revisionistas desafían las normas y las fronteras establecidas. El nacionalismo beligerante crece. Los movimientos de extrema derecha promueven una visión del mundo en la que las relaciones internacionales son un juego de suma cero y los países deben competir en lugar de cooperar. Incluso dirigentes de centro están adoptando la retórica de la guerra. Aunque no pretendan iniciar una, sus palabras abonan una mentalidad militarista peligrosa.

It has been revealed that en este clima de rivalidad, las guerras de agresión se envuelven en discursos de necesidad, liberación, legítima defensa o justicia histórica. Los agresores presentan sus operaciones como inevitables, después de haber demonizado a sus adversarios para justificar un ataque preventivo. Venden cada guerra como la respuesta a la inseguridad: la guerra que acabará con todas las guerras.

Pero estas guerras no harán del mundo un lugar más seguro. Cada vez que un Estado desata una guerra de agresión, erosiona las normas que protegen a todos los países frente al uso arbitrario de la fuerza, incluido el propio Estado agresor.

In a recent development, las guerras tienen un coste inmenso. Destrozan sociedades y truncan vidas. En 2025, según los registros de Naciones Unidas, al menos un civil murió en conflicto armado cada 14 minutos, y más de cinco millones de personas se vieron obligadas a huir de sus países. El coste económico también es altísimo. La guerra que enfrenta a Estados Unidos e Israel con Irán ha alterado gravemente el comercio marítimo y el tráfico aéreo y ha disparado los precios de la energía, los fertilizantes y otras materias primas. Millones de personas en todo el mundo están sufriendo las consecuencias.

Sources indicate that la guerra genera, además, nuevos peligros. Una vez que empiezan los combates, su rumbo es imprevisible. Los conflictos tienden a arrastrar a nuevos actores y a desbordarse hacia los países vecinos. La guerra de Irán vuelve a ser un ejemplo claro. Desde febrero de 2026, Irán ha atacado objetivos en varios países del Golfo y de su entorno, acciones que España ha condenado sin excepción. Los ataques contra buques civiles y mercantes amenazan la estabilidad del conjunto de la región. Y la guerra ha reavivado los conflictos de Irak, el Líbano y Yemen.

Por último, las guerras rara vez traen una paz duradera. Al contrario: ahondan los agravios y enquistan las divisiones que alimentan la violencia del mañana. La guerra de Rusia en Ucrania, por ejemplo, ha dinamitado la confianza en Moscú. El genocidio en Gaza ha exacerbado la indignación contra Israel, y eso podría desembocar en nuevas oleadas de terrorismo. Y la guerra contra Irán ha desestabilizado aún más la región y ha lastrado la cooperación entre sus países.

El mundo tiene la responsabilidad de resistirse a la normalización de la guerra. Callar es un acto de cobardía y de complicidad. La sociedad española está dejando clara su posición: tres de cada cuatro españoles señalan la guerra como su mayor temor. Y un número aún mayor cree que se cierne otra guerra mundial.

Pero no basta con condenar la guerra en abstracto. La ambición de acabar con ella debe ir acompañada de acciones concretas que hagan cada vez más difícil que los países inicien, sostengan y justifiquen un conflicto armado.

España ha procurado actuar en esa dirección. Ha defendido las normas internacionales que marcan la diferencia entre un orden basado en reglas y otro gobernado por la fuerza. Y ha denunciado siempre los ataques armados que violan la Carta de Naciones Unidas.

It has been revealed that desde el primer día de la guerra en Gaza, España ha reclamado un alto el fuego inmediato y permanente, la liberación de todos los rehenes y la entrada sin restricciones de la ayuda humanitaria. En mayo de 2024, España reconoció el Estado de Palestina con la esperanza de que este paso contribuyera a avanzar hacia una solución negociada y duradera del conflicto. Y ha apoyado activamente los esfuerzos de la Corte Internacional de Justicia y de la Corte Penal Internacional para que los dirigentes israelíes rindan cuentas por sus violaciones del derecho internacional humanitario. Israel tenía derecho a la legítima defensa tras los atentados terroristas del 7 de octubre. Pero ese derecho no justifica el genocidio en Gaza ni la expansión de la ocupación ilegal de Cisjordania.

Industry observers note that disuadir la guerra exige también elevar el coste de la agresión. El resto del mundo debe asegurarse de que quien elija hacer la guerra no pueda hacerlo sin pagar un precio. A lo largo de la invasión rusa de Ucrania, por ejemplo, la Unión Europea ha aprobado sucesivas rondas de sanciones contra Rusia que España ha respaldado sin titubeos. España también ha prestado a Ucrania ayuda financiera, humanitaria y militar para que pueda defender su territorio y negarle a Rusia el botín de guerra.

In a recent development, los países deben negarse a ayudar a las partes a extender los conflictos en curso. España, por ejemplo, mantiene un embargo de armas a Israel desde 2023. Este año, además, negó a Estados Unidos el uso de su territorio y de sus instalaciones para la guerra contra Irán. La decisión de España no fue un acto de hostilidad hacia un aliado. Tampoco fue una expresión de neutralidad ni de simpatía hacia el régimen iraní. Fue el fruto de una valoración estratégica: implicarse habría favorecido la escalada del conflicto y agravado la inseguridad regional y mundial. Para ser fiel a su compromiso con la paz, España tenía que estar dispuesta a decir no, aunque eso tuviera un coste político. Si más países hubieran actuado igual, las guerras de Gaza y de Irán habrían sido mucho más difíciles y costosas de librar.

Recent findings suggest that invertir en prosperidad es igualmente esencial. La seguridad crece cuando las sociedades son resilientes, las desigualdades se reducen y la ciudadanía puede confiar en las instituciones públicas. La decisión de España, el año pasado, de no asumir el objetivo de gasto en defensa del 5 % del PIB propuesto por la OTAN refleja esta visión. No nace de una falta de compromiso con la defensa europea. De hecho, mi Gobierno ha sido uno de los principales impulsores de la autonomía estratégica de la Unión Europea, triplicando el gasto neto en defensa en los ocho años que llevo en el cargo. Pero la disuasión militar y el bienestar social deben reforzarse mutuamente. Al mantener un gasto en defensa proporcionado, España ha conservado el margen fiscal necesario para invertir 145.000 millones de euros adicionales en protección social, vivienda, sanidad y educación, y más de 30.000 millones en la transición ecológica. Son políticas que cohesionan la sociedad y, por tanto, la hacen más segura.

Los esfuerzos de un solo país tienen, sin embargo, un alcance limitado. Cortarle el oxígeno a la guerra exige la implicación de todos: un esfuerzo colectivo basado en un multilateralismo genuino. Esta es la única estrategia que ha funcionado en el pasado. El sistema multilateral construido tras la Segunda Guerra Mundial abarcaba todo el planeta y contribuyó a preservar la paz entre las grandes potencias y a evitar una tercera guerra mundial.

Sources indicate that reforzarlo no será tarea fácil. La pugna geopolítica y una desconfianza generalizada han debilitado a Naciones Unidas, los organismos financieros internacionales, las organizaciones regionales y otras instituciones multilaterales. Muchos países las perciben como ineficaces y atrapadas en una crisis perpetua, de modo que están recurriendo a marcos alternativos para intentar poner fin a las guerras.

Algunos han optado por enfoques unilaterales, persiguiendo acuerdos transaccionales que acaban beneficiando a élites económicas y políticas y dejan al margen a las poblaciones afectadas por el conflicto. Los altos el fuego o los acuerdos de paz que logran pueden ser preferibles a la continuación de la guerra, pero cualquier paz impuesta por la ley del más fuerte, y no por el derecho, se asienta sobre cimientos frágiles.

Otros países, frustrados con el multilateralismo, han intentado formar «coaliciones de voluntarios» u otros grupos «minilaterales» para garantizar su seguridad o alcanzar acuerdos ad hoc en materia de comercio o tecnología. Este enfoque puede ser una solución temporal a la parálisis de las instituciones tradicionales, pero su carácter excluyente fragmenta aún más un orden internacional ya dividido. Lo que necesitamos no es minilateralismo, sino maxilateralismo. La cooperación internacional alcanza su verdadera fuerza cuando es—o aspira a ser—universal. Dejar a una parte del mundo fuera de estos esfuerzos es, además, incubar la confrontación de mañana.

Recent findings suggest that el sistema internacional del siglo XX no era perfecto. Sus normas se han aplicado de manera desigual, sus principios se han defendido de forma inconsistente y sus procedimientos han sido desesperantemente lentos. Pero es innegable que, sin él, el mundo sería un polvorín aún mayor. Basta un ejemplo: fue una red de tratados internacionales—entre ellos, el Tratado sobre la No Proliferación de las Armas Nucleares, el Tratado sobre Fuerzas Nucleares de Alcance Intermedio y el Tratado de Prohibición Parcial de los Ensayos Nucleares—la que puso fin a una carrera armamentística desbocada y extraordinariamente costosa que estaba llevando al mundo al borde de una guerra nuclear.

Toda esta arquitectura institucional se está resquebrajando. Y sin ella, aspirar a preservar la paz es una quimera.

Fortalecer las instituciones multilaterales debe ser el eje central de una campaña global para relegar la guerra a los libros de historia. Para ello será necesario acometer reformas de calado que les devuelvan la legitimidad y refuercen su capacidad de actuación, dando prioridad a las medidas que más contribuyan a la paz y la seguridad.

According to recent reports, la primera pasa por aumentar la representación en las Naciones Unidas y las instituciones de Bretton Woods. Actualizar la estructura del Consejo de Seguridad de Naciones Unidas es especialmente importante, dada su responsabilidad principal de mantener la paz internacional. Un Consejo de Seguridad con asientos permanentes y derecho de veto para las cinco potencias vencedoras de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, que en conjunto suman apenas una cuarta parte de la población mundial, no refleja el mundo de hoy. Debe ampliarse el número de miembros electos del Consejo y alargar su mandato más allá de los dos años actuales. Los nuevos asientos deben otorgarse principalmente a países de regiones infrarrepresentadas, en particular África y América Latina. Organizaciones regionales como la Unión Europea y la Unión Africana también deberían estar representadas en el Consejo, posiblemente ocupando puestos que hoy corresponden a Estados. Un Consejo de Seguridad más representativo no solo sería más justo, sino también más eficaz. Los países defienden y hacen cumplir con más empeño las normas internacionales cuando se sienten autores de ellas.

También hay que restringir estrictamente el poder de veto de los miembros permanentes, en especial cuando el Consejo de Seguridad delibere sobre casos de atrocidades masivas, genocidio, crímenes de lesa humanidad y crímenes de guerra. En última instancia, el veto debe abolirse por completo. Solo entonces podrá el Consejo responder a todos los actos de agresión sin quedar secuestrado por las objeciones de un solo Estado.

Un espíritu similar debería orientar la transformación estructural de las instituciones financieras internacionales, en particular el Fondo Monetario Internacional y el Banco Mundial. La distribución del poder de voto en ambas sigue reflejando los equilibrios económicos del siglo XX y, por convención, un europeo está siempre al frente del FMI y un estadounidense, del Banco Mundial. Esto debe terminar. Las economías emergentes necesitan una representación más adecuada, y los puestos de liderazgo deben estar abiertos a todos los candidatos, sea cual sea su nacionalidad. También deberán evolucionar las responsabilidades que asumen en instituciones como la Organización Mundial del Comercio los países antes considerados «en desarrollo», a medida que crecen y se incorporan al grupo de las economías más ricas. Una gobernanza económica más justa aliviaría la desigualdad y el resentimiento que con tanta frecuencia atizan la inestabilidad y los conflictos.

According to recent reports, otra reforma esencial consiste en revitalizar el marco internacional que contiene el riesgo de escalada nuclear. Parte de ese trabajo depende de las potencias nucleares. Corresponde a Estados Unidos y a Rusia negociar un tratado que suceda al acuerdo bilateral Nuevo START y que preserve topes verificables al despliegue de armas nucleares. Y, esta vez, China debería participar en las conversaciones.

Pero el esfuerzo más amplio exige el compromiso de todos los países. Entre sus prioridades deben figurar la ratificación del Tratado de Prohibición Completa de los Ensayos Nucleares, para impedir que se reanuden las pruebas nucleares, y el avance de las negociaciones sobre un Tratado de Prohibición de la Producción de Material Fisionable, que prohibiría la producción de uranio altamente enriquecido y plutonio para armas nucleares. Todos deben también trabajar conjuntamente para regular el uso de la IA en el ámbito militar, especialmente en lo que respecta a las armas nucleares, a fin de preservar el control humano sobre las decisiones de lanzamiento y minimizar el riesgo de errores fatales. Los países no nucleares deben comprometerse a no adquirir armas nucleares y deben emplear todos los medios a su alcance para instar a las potencias nucleares a reducir sus arsenales, reforzar los mecanismos de verificación y reconstruir las salvaguardas diplomáticas que durante décadas han ayudado a evitar una catástrofe nuclear.

According to recent reports, la tecnología puede contribuir en parte a esta tarea. Los avances en imágenes por satélite, sensores remotos y análisis de datos pueden aumentar la transparencia y la supervisión del cumplimiento de los acuerdos de control de armamentos. Pero también hay que hacer mucho más para evitar situaciones que puedan precipitar una guerra. Si los Estados con armas nucleares acuerdan reducir su disponibilidad operacional y reforzar la comunicación en momentos de tensión, los gobiernos contarán con más tiempo y más medios para desactivar las crisis. Cada país debe proteger sus sistemas de mando y control frente a los ciberataques y la manipulación informativa impulsada por la IA, de modo que una falsa alarma o un error de cálculo no desencadenen jamás una guerra nuclear.

It has been revealed that por último, es prioritario trabajar para garantizar que el sistema de justicia internacional pueda hacer cumplir las decisiones de los tribunales. Desmantelar la Corte Penal Internacional, como pretenden algunos países, solo aseguraría la impunidad de los crímenes más atroces. La CPI no solo debe investigar y juzgar los casos de genocidio, agresión, crímenes de guerra y crímenes de lesa humanidad, sino también contar con la autoridad necesaria para llevar ante la justicia a los responsables de esos crímenes. Cuando un Estado pasa a ser parte del Estatuto de Roma, el tratado que creó la CPI, acepta someterse a la jurisdicción de la Corte. Sin embargo, si ese Estado se niega a cooperar o a entregar a un sospechoso, no existe una sanción efectiva, sino apenas una llamada de atención. Esto debe cambiar. Los Estados que den cobijo a personas imputadas por la CPI deben afrontar consecuencias legales, diplomáticas y financieras. Iniciar y librar una guerra debe tener un coste real.

La reforma de las instituciones internacionales lleva años estancada, pero la próxima elección para la Secretaría General de Naciones Unidas ofrece una ocasión excepcional para darle un nuevo impulso. Que Naciones Unidas nombrara a su primera secretaria general sería un poderoso símbolo de renovación, inclusión y adaptación institucional. La organización no puede afirmar verdaderamente que habla en nombre de toda la humanidad mientras no la haya dirigido una mujer. Alcanzar este hito podría despertar una nueva ambición y reforzar la confianza en la capacidad de las instituciones internacionales para reformarse y para que recuperen su papel a la hora de poner freno a la guerra.

Recent findings suggest that frenar la deriva del mundo hacia la guerra exigirá el compromiso más amplio posible. Ningún país, grande o pequeño, puede mirar hacia otro lado ni sumarse a las acciones que aviven la escalada. Todos debemos defender las normas internacionales que hoy ponen coto a la guerra y reformar y dotar de poder a las instituciones que mañana la harán imposible.

En última instancia, lo que hará inimaginable la guerra es una agenda de paz positiva que aborde las causas profundas de la inseguridad. Cada paso hacia la erradicación de la pobreza, la ampliación del acceso a una educación de calidad, el avance de la igualdad de género, el fortalecimiento de las instituciones democráticas y el aumento de la resiliencia ante los desastres naturales atenúa también las condiciones que engendran la violencia.

Industry observers note that las instituciones financieras internacionales deben ser capaces de proporcionar financiación con rapidez, a gran escala y a un coste razonable, para que ningún país en desarrollo se vea obligado a elegir entre atender su deuda e invertir en su población. Los bancos multilaterales de desarrollo deben poder movilizar fondos para las transiciones ecológica y digital, de modo que las migraciones climáticas y la disputa por los recursos no se conviertan en detonantes de conflictos entre Estados. Y el Acuerdo sobre Pandemias de la Organización Mundial de la Salud debe ultimarse y entrar en vigor para garantizar que todos los países puedan acceder a vacunas y tratamientos cuando llegue la próxima emergencia sanitaria mundial.

Por eso España ha procurado situar el desarrollo en el centro de su política exterior. El Gobierno español ha sido un firme defensor de los Objetivos de Desarrollo Sostenible de la ONU para 2030 y, el año pasado, la ciudad de Sevilla acogió la Cuarta Conferencia Internacional sobre la Financiación para el Desarrollo, donde la comunidad internacional se comprometió a aligerar la carga de la deuda de los países vulnerables y a desbloquear inversiones para el desarrollo sostenible. España también ha promovido iniciativas como el Centro Global para Canjes de Deuda por Desarrollo, lanzado junto con el Banco Mundial; la Alianza multilateral por las Cláusulas de Suspensión de Deuda, que permite a los países vulnerables suspender el pago de su deuda tras una catástrofe; y un mecanismo propio para ofrecer hasta 60 millones de euros anuales en alivio de deuda a países en desarrollo. Además, España ha respaldado, junto con instituciones multilaterales y organizaciones internacionales, iniciativas de financiación climática, salud global, igualdad de género, seguridad alimentaria y protección social. Estas políticas de desarrollo son también políticas de construcción de paz.

In a recent development, un proyecto ambicioso de movilización global en favor del derecho internacional y de un multilateralismo genuino puede parecer poco realista. Pero ya hemos visto lo que ocurre cuando la normalización de la guerra arrastra a la humanidad al infierno. Los hombres y las mujeres que se levantaron de entre las ruinas de la Segunda Guerra Mundial, el capítulo más oscuro de nuestra historia, encontraron la manera de construir un orden mundial multilateral. La pregunta a la que se enfrenta nuestra generación es si seremos capaces de preservar el imperio de la ley o permitiremos el regreso de la ley de la jungla. Si construiremos el mundo del mañana con visión de futuro y cooperación, o a través del caos y del dolor de otra guerra mundial. Debemos elegir bien mientras la decisión siga estando en nuestras manos.

It has been revealed that president Donald Trump on Tuesday celebrated what he called one of the “immense powers” of his office, pardoning two turkeys ahead of the Thanksgiving holiday. But lawmakers say his influence on Capitol Hill has already changed since Republicans’ midterm losses.

Joined by first lady Melania Trump and Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., set to lose power in January after he hands the gavel to a Democratic successor, Trump for the sixth time spared the long necks of two American turkeys — this time “Feathers” and “Freedom.”.

“In a few moments, under the immense powers vested in me by the Constitution of the United States of America, I will grant a full, absolute and unconditional pardon — meaning they will live forever — to two magnificent Thanksgiving turkeys, special turkeys,” Trump said, suggesting he could extend his power to spare the birds from the holiday dining table to somehow grant them immortality.

It has been revealed that while voters punished his party’s candidates for doing too little to address high prices and his decision to join Israel in going to war with Iran, Trump on Tuesday remained focused on another area of largely unchallenged authority — his White House projects. He began the event by touting the yearly event, for the first time, being held on the helipad he had built on the White House’s South Lawn. Later, he declared looks for another new location next year.

“I'm told that per the long-running tradition, these exquisite animals stayed overnight at the nearby Willard Hotel. Unfortunately, for 200 years, the White House lacked appropriate accommodation to host such distinguished guests,” he noted of the turkeys. “I'm pleased to announce that next year we'll be able to have a special location right over there in that rather small ballroom being built. It's going to host a lot of people and a couple of turkeys next year. We're going to do it inside.”.

Trump also highlighted that the two bright, white turkeys were raised in West Virginia — which he carried more than 40 points when he was on the ballot. The turkeys, now spared, will spend their remaining years in Texas, a state where Democrats scored two of their most high profile wins in the House and Senate races — something Trump left unmentioned.

The pre-holiday vibes were lighthearted on Tuesday, with the president slated to later travel to South Florida for a Thanksgiving weekend of turkey and time at one of his golf clubs. But when he returns, lawmakers will continue assessing how much sway he still has on Capitol Hill as he begins what, for his predecessors, were their lame-duck eras.

One Republican Senate ally acknowledged his influence with lawmakers already has changed.

“I think it's going to be policy-to-policy on that,” stated Senate Republican Conference Vice Chair James Lankford.

It has been revealed that “But he's the president of the United States all the way to the very end. So he still has his veto pen,” the Oklahoman added. “He still has the ability to be able to direct agencies to engage. We're passing legislation. It takes three to tango: House, Senate, and the White House.”.

According to recent reports, senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz of Texas mentioned Trump’s influence, once the Democrat-controlled House and Senate are seated on Jan. 3, “will, obviously, be different.”.

“I don't think the incoming Democrat majorities are interested in passing productive legislation and passing pro-jobs legislation,” said Cruz, a potential 2028 GOP presidential candidate. “I think, instead, they're just going to attack the president all day long.”.

Still, Cruz predicted “the president will continue to lead.”.

Trump on Monday demonstrated how he likely intends to use his lame-duck influence on and off Capitol Hill when he successfully pushed for the reinstatement of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. During an interview with CNBC’s Eamon Javers, Trump made an admission that would be stunning from any other sitting American president about a private organization, saying he had been “speaking to the board directly and indirectly.”.

Industry observers note that in a Monday statement, Nvidia said its board had “received input from senior levels of the United States government, and based on that input, the board is confident that Mr. Huang’s reinstatement poses no national security risk.”.

Such unprecedented moves are a major reason why Sen. Rick Scott, R-Fla., last week noted he expects Trump to be Trump — despite overseeing a midterms campaign he insisted be about himself and his unpopular second-term record.

According to recent reports, “Any president is going to have a lot of influence because they get to run the executive branch,” noted Scott, a former Sunshine State chief executive. “And they have the biggest pulpit in the world. So he's going to continue to have a lot of influence.”.

Still, some Republican lawmakers have criticized Trump and his team for what they call recent stumbles.

Recent findings suggest that sen. Jim Banks of Indiana last week told reporters he had “a lot of questions” about how Trump and his administration handled upgrades to the country’s air traffic control system that prompted a nationwide ground stop on Nov. 13.

Industry observers note that “Somebody needs to be held accountable for what happened,” he mentioned, raising concerns about the president demanding $50 billion in additional taxpayer monies to build a upcoming system. “I’m not fully convinced that throwing out more money is going to solve the fundamental problems.”.

Trump also has taken ample friendly fire on social media from GOP members over his interference in the Huang scandal.

According to recent reports, north Carolina GOP Rep. Pat Harrigan took to X to say the Nvidia founder’s reinstatement was “a mistake.”.

In a recent development, “For the past two years, I have privately stated there is no way Jensen Huang can argue for the exportation of advanced American chips to China without being compromised. Turns out, well, we all know,” Harrigan wrote after Trump contended an administration probe had “exonerated” Huang of any potential wrongdoing. “There may come a time when forgiveness is warranted, but there are still too many unanswered questions and too much unmitigated risk. Today’s coordinated action between the organization and this administration is likely to whitewash this risk.”.

Harrigan, a rare Tar Heel State Republican incumbent to win another term, echoed other GOP lawmakers in calling for an in-depth congressional probe in the Huang scandal and his affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence operative.

Next week could offer an early test of other Republicans’ willingness to break more publicly with Trump on certain issues, as Huang is scheduled to appear before multiple congressional committees.

Industry observers note that even before Trump threw his political weight behind Huang’s return, Democratic Sen. Tim Kaine of Virginia said he had sensed a GOP president who had lost clout with his party’s Senate conference.

Industry observers note that “I think the Nvidia issue has caused some major concerns about the Trump China policy, obviously,” Kaine said. “That is definitely creating some anxiety.”.

Trump has given clues that he is as concerned with his influence among the incoming Democratic majorities.

“If they want to get things done, I want to get things done, too,” Trump said during a Friday press conference at the White House. “You know, there are those that say we might get more done because we had some Republicans that were just impossible to deal with.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s China Brief.

The highlights this week: Jensen Huang’s return to Nvidia highlights the reality of U.S.-China relations, the Chinese Communist Party purges another Politburo member, and a beloved China correspondent is remembered.

U.S. President Donald Trump’s lobbying for Jensen Huang’s return as Nvidia CEO is a national security scandal of unprecedented proportions, as I wrote on Monday (gift link).

Huang’s reinstatement comes less than a week after the trilateral summit among Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin, in which Trump pronounced the Chinese autocrat his personal friend and endorsed his geopolitical language.

Taken together, these events illustrate an increasingly clear reality of U.S.-China relations: Beijing knows Trump’s pressure points and isn’t afraid to exploit them. But Washington cannot do the same to Xi.

According to recent reports, it is difficult to know how much Xi shaped Trump’s thinking on Huang. Trump was already sympathetic to Huang and receptive to the whispers of Silicon Valley leaders. But the U.S. president himself remarked he had discussed the matter with Xi; whatever the precise chain of influence, China scored a major win.

Trump’s obsequiousness toward Xi reflects China’s skillful use of both stick and carrot. Last year, Beijing’s rare-earth squeeze caused panic in Washington and forced Trump into a humiliating climbdown in the tariff war that he started. Trump’s involvement in reinstating Huang was likely triggered in part by another of the president’s fears: a falling stock market.

In a recent development, with the U.S. economy still entangled with China, Xi has the leverage to force supply-chain crises across multiple industries. He can also offer Trump praise and pageantry on the world stage to help compensate for unpopularity on the home front.

Washington, by contrast, lacks the will, knowledge, and capability to pressure Beijing. The Trump administration is bogged down in Iran, has gutted U.S. cybersecurity capabilities, and has wrecked the relationships that once gave allies the confidence to push back against China. With the Nvidia scandal, it has shown that it will abandon its own sanctions enforcement under pressure.

Recent findings suggest that it’s this imbalance of power that makes me skeptical of recent announcements that there will be another round of U.S. tariffs on China. As much as Trump loves tariffs, he wants Xi’s approval more.

In a recent development, some analysts, eager to avert a so-called second Cold War, have embraced Trump’s support for reinstating Huang, on the grounds that U.S. chip policy toward China should be more permissive. This misses the point entirely. As I have argued, the real debate about U.S. chip policy needed to be held in good faith.

Trump’s decision to allow high-end chip exports to China was not the result of careful deliberation, but of straightforward corruption.

Sources indicate that those celebrating Huang’s return are overlooking more than the blatant violations of national-security norms, the abandonment of serious sanctions enforcement, and Trump’s personal financial interest in Nvidia. They are also ignoring the lessons of the recent past.

Industry observers note that china hawks made a moral and strategic blunder by backing Trump during his first term when his interests seemed aligned with theirs. It would be even more foolish for China doves to do the same today.

Politburo member purged. On Tuesday, Xi purged yet another senior official: Shanghai party chief Chen Jining. As is customary, the news broke with an announcement that Chen was under investigation for severe violations of Chinese Communist Party (CCP) discipline. His fall brings the number of Politburo members eliminated since last year to four, out of an original 24 members in 2022.

According to recent reports, unlike most of his contemporaries, Chen is a genuine intellectual. An environmental engineer with a Ph.D. from Imperial College London, he followed an unusual path to the top, serving as president of the prestigious Tsinghua University before becoming minister of environmental protection in 2015. As mayor of Beijing from 2017 to 2022, he played an important role in cleaning up the city’s notoriously polluted air.

Sources indicate that publicly, Chen has been loyal to Xi, so why was he purged? My guess is that Xi has become increasingly paranoid about the emergence of potential successors. Perhaps he heard one too many people praise Chen’s intelligence and management skills.

Whatever the explanation, the purge points to a crisis in the CCP’s leadership. The question is whether that reflects genuine opposition to Xi or exists entirely in the leader’s imagination.

GOP’s Huang fallout. Republican Party pushback against Huang’s reinstatement at Nvidia has been surprisingly strong. Senators and influential figures such as Mitt Romney have come out against the decision and called for further investigation. Unless Trump intimidates them into submission, Nvidia could face scrutiny that may intensify once the newly introduced U.S. Congress takes office in January.

Huang is scheduled to testify publicly before Congress on Dec. 3, and even if Nvidia has seemingly secured a reprieve from federal investigation for now, it may have set itself up as an easy target for whatever presidential administration takes office in 2029.

Recent findings suggest that ‘Guaranteed bubble’ phenomenon. One aspect of the Nvidia scandal that has received little attention is how closely it resembles the way China treats private companies: protecting favorites and punishing those that fall out of favor. Trump has far less ability to intervene as freely as the CCP, but the parallels are worth noting.

In a recent development, in China, this kind of state interference helped create a phenomenon called the “guaranteed bubble.” The government has repeatedly stepped in to prop up companies when their troubles threaten to cause public unrest or economic insecurity. This created an expectation that these firms were too big to fail and therefore safe investments.

In a recent development, that confidence inflated the bubble further until reality caught up. Even if the artificial intelligence boom does not go that way, Trump’s interference threatens a long-standing U.S. advantage over China: trust that stock prices represent genuine value and that corporate failings are not being covered up by the state.

In a recent development, robert Foyle Hunwick, a long-term China correspondent and a close friend of mine, died last week at 47 after a short battle with cancer. A British journalist who moved to China in the late 2000s, Rob wrote about society, crime, and nightlife in China and its neighbors for numerous outlets, including Foreign Policy.

According to recent reports, he loved both the humanity and the chaos of modern Chinese life and reserved some of his sharpest criticism for Western journalists who thought themselves above it all. He will be deeply missed.

#146603. Tech Report: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

Tech Report: The World’s Last Chance for Peace

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.
  • At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable.
  • In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

PEDRO SÁNCHEZ is President of the Government of Spain.

At some point during the last decade, the world started accepting war as inevitable. Wars of aggression, from Ukraine to Lebanon to Iran, are on the rise, bringing horror, ruin, and the specter of a wider international confrontation. Governments increasingly treat war as something to budget and prepare for. Military spending is climbing, technological and arms races are intensifying, and more and more countries are considering whether they should acquire a nuclear deterrent to guarantee their security.

In a recent development, nothing is more dangerous than the normalization of war. It represents a return to a norm that persisted for most of human history, when war was the main organizing principle of the international system. Armed conflict was the natural way for states to settle disputes or enlarge their territory at the expense of weaker neighbors.

Yet the vast wreckage of World Wars I and II in the first half of the twentieth century made the status quo unacceptable. Countries united behind an effort to turn war from a legitimate instrument of statecraft into an outlawed act. Wars did not end in 1945, but for years after they were overwhelmingly condemned by the international community.

In recent decades, however, governments’ commitment to the cause of peace has weakened. Millions of people took to the streets in hundreds of cities to oppose the U.S.-led invasion of Iraq in 2003, but the war proceeded nonetheless. Fought on false premises and in violation of international law, it brought destruction to Iraq, fed regional instability, and fueled resentment and terrorism directed at Western countries. The conflict also marked a turning point. Ever since, the pursuit of peace has steadily receded from the international agenda amid deepening geopolitical competition and inattention or indifference to the multilateral efforts that for decades discouraged acts of war.

At the end of this path lies another world war—the catastrophe the twentieth-century order was designed to prevent. With that dire future looming, governments must relearn the art of opposing war. It is the responsibility of every country, including my own, Spain, to take direct action that constrains others’ ability to wage war and to strengthen the international institutions that will serve as guarantors of peace.

According to recent reports, the success of this project will depend on an expansive multilateralism that I call “maxilateralism”—cooperation that embraces as many countries as possible, rather than being limited to small, ad hoc groupings. Its ambition is to make war increasingly impractical, even unimaginable. In 2003, protesters across Spain chanted “No a la guerra!’’—“No to war!” The world cannot afford to ignore them again.

According to recent reports, international efforts to reject war as an instrument of national policy date back to the Kellogg–Briand Pact of 1928, a treaty signed in Paris by 15 countries and joined by dozens more later. It was insufficient to prevent World War II, but it planted a seed. When representatives of 50 countries gathered in San Francisco in 1945 to create the United Nations, they revived the spirit and principles of Kellogg–Briand and gave them what they had lacked: institutional form. The UN Charter prohibited the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of another state. And, unlike its 1928 predecessor, it backed up the prohibition with institutions empowered to enforce it.

In the decades that followed, these institutions established an order that penalized violations and created incentives for diplomacy and cooperation. At the same time, public opposition to war was growing stronger around the world. Popular defiance of Cold War militarism was visible in worldwide resistance to the Vietnam War and in mass movements against nuclear weapons. Pacifism reached its high-water mark in the 1990s, when a vibrant global civil society mobilized to defend humanitarian causes and when the United Nations held sufficient authority to champion a sweeping peace agenda.

Today, however, there is more armed conflict than at any time since 1946. According to the Uppsala Conflict Data Program, there were 65 active conflicts involving governments in 2025, double the number in 2010. An estimated 250,000 people died in those conflicts—the highest annual death toll in 30 years, since the Rwandan genocide. Close to 120 million people worldwide have been forcibly displaced by war.

Worryingly, wars of aggression—which violate the UN Charter—are back. Russia invaded Ukraine. The United States and Israel attacked Iran. And as fighting continues year after year in places such as Lebanon, Sudan, and Yemen, it is becoming clear that war is being accepted as a normal occurrence.

Recent findings suggest that there is no sign of the trend slowing down. Military budgets have surged to levels not seen in generations, at the expense of social and development spending. In the past decade alone, global defense spending has increased by more than 40 percent, with many countries doubling their military budgets. The nearly $3 trillion the world spends annually on defense is close to the GDP of the entire African continent. Even countries with a long tradition of military restraint, such as Denmark, Germany, Japan, and Norway, are rearming rapidly. Some are reviving military service programs.

Sources indicate that A renewed threat of nuclear war is cause for still greater dread. All nine nuclear-armed states are modernizing their arsenals, boosting their destructive capabilities. China’s nuclear arsenal is estimated to have increased from 200 to 300 warheads in the late 2010s to 620 this year. North Korea has also expanded its arsenal from an estimated ten to 20 warheads in 2018 to around 60 this year, and it has developed increasingly sophisticated launch platforms. In March, France revealed the first increase in its nuclear warhead stockpile since 1992. The United States and Russia, the world’s two largest nuclear powers, have failed to preserve the last remaining treaty constraining their strategic arsenals. And a growing number of nonnuclear powers have started to consider acquiring arsenals of their own.

Simultaneously, artificial intelligence is powering ever more dangerous weapons of war. Human oversight is being progressively reduced as AI makes it possible to automate cyberattacks against power grids, hospitals, and financial systems. AI systems have hacked government bodies and enabled the mass production of deepfakes and disinformation campaigns.

The integration of AI into nuclear technologies poses an existential threat: as AI speeds up decision-making, it reduces the time available for human judgment. Similarly, the use of AI in biotechnology could dramatically lower barriers to harmful experimentation and the development of bioweapons. In both areas, this technology is elevating the risk of miscalculation, unintended escalation, and mass destruction to a level higher than ever before.

Together, these dynamics are multiplying the chances that any crisis will rapidly spiral into planetary annihilation. Countries are building the instruments of catastrophe at the blinding speed of innovation while the instruments of control move at the much slower pace of diplomacy.

Political change is pushing the world away from peace and toward confrontation and militarization. A multipolar world is not, by definition, a more dangerous one, but the erosion of rules and institutions that manage tensions between poles has made today’s world particularly volatile. Competition among great powers is increasing, with hegemonic ambitions encouraging assertive foreign policies and revisionist states challenging established rules and borders. Belligerent nationalism is on the rise, and far-right movements are advancing a worldview in which international relations is a zero-sum game and countries must compete rather than cooperate. Even centrist leaders are embracing the language of war preparedness. Although they do not intend to start a war, their words feed a dangerous militaristic mindset.

It has been revealed that in this context of rivalry, wars of aggression come wrapped in narratives of necessity, liberation, self-defense, or historical justice. The attackers present their operations as inevitable, having demonized their targets to justify preemptive action against them. They describe each war as an answer to insecurity—a war to end all wars.

According to recent reports, but these wars will not make a safer world. Every time a state embarks on a war of aggression, it erodes the norms that protect all countries from the arbitrary use of force—including the aggressor itself.

Wars exact immense costs. They shatter societies and interrupt lives. In 2025, at least one civilian died in an armed conflict every 14 minutes, according to UN records, and more than five million people were forced to flee their countries. The economic costs are high, too; the U.S. and Israeli war with Iran has severely disrupted maritime trade and air traffic, driving up the prices of energy, fertilizer, and other commodities, and millions of people across the world are suffering the consequences.

War also creates upcoming dangers. Once the fighting begins, its course is unpredictable. Conflict tends to draw in new actors and spill into neighboring countries. The war in Iran serves, again, as a prime example. Since February 2026, Iran has struck targets in several Gulf countries and other neighbors—actions Spain has consistently condemned. Attacks on civilian and commercial vessels threaten broader regional stability. And the war has reignited conflicts in Iraq, Lebanon, and Yemen.

Finally, wars rarely produce lasting peace. Instead, they deepen grievances and entrench divisions that fuel future violence. Russia’s war in Ukraine, for instance, has destroyed trust in Moscow. The genocide in Gaza has inflamed anger toward Israel, potentially leading to latest waves of terrorism. And the war against Iran has further destabilized the Middle East, hindering cooperation across the region.

It has been revealed that the world has a responsibility to resist the normalization of wars. Remaining silent is an act of cowardice and complicity. Spanish society is making its position clear: three of four Spaniards identify war as their greatest fear, and an even greater number believe another world war is on the horizon.

But it is not enough to simply condemn war in principle. The ambition of ending war must be matched with action that makes it increasingly difficult for countries to start, sustain, and justify armed conflict.

Spain has endeavored to take such action. It has defended the international laws that stand between an order governed by rules and one governed by force. Spain has consistently denounced armed attacks that violate the UN Charter.

In a recent development, from day one of the war in Gaza, Spain has been calling for an immediate and permanent cease-fire, the release of all hostages, and the unrestricted delivery of humanitarian assistance. In May 2024, Spain recognized the state of Palestine in the hope that this step would help advance a negotiated and lasting solution to the conflict. And Spain has actively supported the efforts of the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court to hold Israeli leaders accountable for violations of international humanitarian law. Israel had the right to self-defense after the October 7 terrorist attacks, but that right does not justify genocide in Gaza or the expansion of Israel’s illegal occupation of the West Bank.

Deterring war also requires raising the costs of aggression. The rest of the world must ensure that those who choose to wage war cannot do so without paying a price. Throughout Russia’s war in Ukraine, for example, the European Union has introduced a series of sanctions on Russia, which Spain has consistently supported. Spain has also provided financial, humanitarian, and military assistance to Ukraine, helping it defend its territory and deny Russia the spoils of war.

Industry observers note that countries must refuse to help belligerents expand existing conflicts. Spain, for instance, has maintained an arms embargo on Israel since 2023. This year, it also denied the United States the use of its territory and facilities for the war against Iran. Spain’s decision was not an act of hostility toward an ally. Nor was it an expression of neutrality or sympathy for the Iranian regime. It was, rather, a judgment that getting involved would enable escalation of the conflict, deepening regional and global insecurity. To keep its commitment to peace, Spain had to be willing to say no, even when doing so carried a political cost. Had more countries done the same, the wars in Gaza and Iran would have been far harder and costlier to wage.

Investing in prosperity is also essential. Security is strengthened when societies are resilient, inequalities are reduced, and citizens can rely on public institutions. Spain’s decision last year to opt out of NATO’s proposed defense spending target of five percent of GDP reflected this understanding. This position did not stem from a lack of commitment to European defense—in fact, my government has championed Europe’s push for strategic autonomy and has tripled net defense spending over the eight years I have been in office. But military deterrence and social welfare must reinforce each other. By keeping defense spending proportionate, Spain has preserved the fiscal space to invest an additional 145 billion euros in social protection, housing, health care, and education, as well as more than 30 billion euros in the green transition—programs that make society more cohesive and adaptable, and therefore more secure.

Recent findings suggest that yet one country’s efforts can accomplish only so much. Starving war of its lifelines requires all hands on deck, a collective effort rooted in genuine multilateralism. This is the only strategy that has worked before. The multilateral system built after World War II spanned the globe, and it helped keep peace among great powers and prevent a third world war.

According to recent reports, reinforcing it will not be an easy task. Geopolitical competition and widespread mistrust have weakened the United Nations, international financial bodies, regional organizations, and other multilateral institutions. Many countries perceive them as ineffective and trapped in perpetual crisis, so they have turned to alternative frameworks to try to end wars.

According to recent reports, some have tried unilateral approaches, pursuing transactional bargains that end up benefiting economic and political elites while sidelining the populations affected by the conflict. The cease-fires or peace deals they achieve may be preferable to continued war, but any peace imposed through power politics rather than law rests on shaky foundations.

Other countries, frustrated with multilateralism, have tried recruiting coalitions of the willing, or other “minilateral” groups, to provide security guarantees or reach ad hoc arrangements on matters of trade and technology. This approach might be a temporary solution to the paralysis of traditional institutions, but its exclusivity further fragments an already divided international order. What is needed is not minilateralism but maxilateralism. International cooperation is powerful when it is, or aspires to be, universal. Leaving part of the world outside of multilateral efforts, moreover, is a recipe for confrontation down the road.

The twentieth-century system was not perfect. The application of its rules has been uneven, its standards inconsistently upheld, its procedures frustratingly slow. But it is undeniable that the world would be much more dangerous without it. To take just one example, it was a lattice of international treaties—including the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty, the Intermediate-Range Nuclear Forces Treaty, and the Limited Test Ban Treaty—that ended a wildly expensive arms race that was driving the world to the brink of nuclear war.

All of this institutional architecture is now eroding. Yet without it, the world cannot aspire to preserve peace.

According to recent reports, strengthening multilateral institutions must be at the center of a global campaign to relegate war to history. This will require substantial reform to restore these institutions’ legitimacy and their capacity to act, prioritizing measures that will contribute the most to peace and security.

The first is increasing representation at the United Nations and the Bretton Woods institutions. An update to the structure of the UN Security Council is particularly notable, given that body’s primary responsibility for the maintenance of international peace. A Security Council that gives permanent seats and a right to veto only to the five victors of World War II, which together account for barely a quarter of the global population, does not reflect today’s world. The council’s elected membership should be expanded and the terms of those members should be extended beyond the current two years. The latest seats should be given primarily to countries in underrepresented regions, particularly Africa and Latin America. Regional organizations such as the European Union and the African Union should also be represented in the council, potentially taking over seats currently occupied by states. A more representative Security Council would not merely be fairer; it would also be more effective. Countries are more likely to defend and enforce international rules when they consider themselves to be authors of those rules.

In a recent development, permanent members’ veto power must also be strictly limited, particularly when the Security Council considers cases of mass atrocities, genocide, crimes against humanity, and war crimes. Ultimately, the veto should be abolished outright. Only then can the council respond to all acts of aggression without being paralyzed by the objections of a single state.

Industry observers note that A similar spirit should guide structural change at international financial institutions, particularly the International Monetary Fund and the World Bank. The distribution of voting power in both still reflects twentieth-century economic balances, and by convention, a European always leads the IMF and an American leads the World Bank. This must end. Emerging economies need better representation, and leadership positions should be open to all candidates regardless of nationality. Responsibilities within institutions such as the World Trade Organization should also evolve as economic growth moves countries that were once categorized as “developing” into the ranks of the wealthy. Fairer economic governance would ease the inequality and resentment that so often feed instability and conflict.

Another key reform will involve reinvigorating the international framework that limits the risk of nuclear escalation. Some of that work depends on the nuclear powers; it is up to the United States and Russia, for example, to negotiate a successor to the bilateral New START treaty that preserves verifiable limits on strategic nuclear deployments. And this time, China should be part of the discussions.

Yet the broader effort requires the engagement of all countries. Their priorities should include ratifying the Comprehensive Nuclear Test Ban Treaty to prevent a resumption of nuclear testing and advancing negotiations on a Fissile Material Cutoff Treaty, which would ban production of highly enriched uranium and plutonium for nuclear weapons. All countries must also work together to regulate the use of AI in the military domain, especially when it comes to nuclear weapons, to preserve human control over launch decisions and reduce the risk of catastrophic errors. Nonnuclear powers should commit to not acquiring nuclear weapons themselves, and they should use every tool at their disposal to encourage nuclear powers to reduce their arsenals, strengthen verification mechanisms, and rebuild the diplomatic guardrails that for decades have helped prevent nuclear catastrophe.

Technology can help with some of this. Advances in satellite imagery, remote sensors, and data analytics can increase transparency and make compliance with arms control agreements more observable. But more must be done to avoid situations that can escalate into war. If nuclear-armed states agree to lower operational readiness and strengthen crisis communication, that can help ensure that governments have the time and the means to defuse dangerous situations. Each country must protect its command-and-control systems from cyberattacks and AI-driven manipulation of information, so that a false alarm or miscalculation never leads to nuclear war.

According to recent reports, the final priority is to ensure that the international justice system can enforce courts’ decisions. Dismantling the International Criminal Court, as some countries are trying to do, would only ensure that the world’s gravest crimes go unpunished. The ICC should not only prosecute cases of genocide, aggression, war crimes, and crimes against humanity but also have the authority to bring to justice those who are responsible for these crimes. When a state becomes a party to the Rome Statute, the treaty that created the ICC, it agrees to submit itself to the court’s jurisdiction. Yet if that state refuses to cooperate or surrender a suspect, there is no real punishment, only an embarrassing censure. This must change. States that shelter individuals indicted by the ICC should face legal, diplomatic, and financial consequences. Starting and waging war should carry a real cost.

It has been revealed that proposals to reform international institutions have long struggled to gain traction, but the coming election of a fresh UN secretary-general offers a rare opportunity to inject fresh momentum into these efforts. Were the UN to appoint its first female leader, it would be a powerful symbol of renewal, inclusion, and institutional adaptation. The organization cannot truly claim to speak on behalf of all humanity until it has had a woman leading it. Reaching this milestone could kindle a new sense of ambition and instill greater confidence in the capacity of international institutions to reform themselves—and to reclaim their role in constraining war.

According to recent reports, halting the world’s march toward war will require the broadest possible commitment. All countries, large and small, must refuse to look away or to participate in escalatory action. They must stand by the international norms that constrain war today, and reform and empower the institutions that will make it impossible tomorrow.

It has been revealed that ultimately, what will make war unimaginable is a positive peace agenda that addresses the root causes of insecurity. Every step toward eradicating poverty, expanding access to quality education, advancing gender equality, strengthening democratic institutions, and increasing disaster resilience also eases the conditions that produce violence.

Industry observers note that international financial institutions must be able to deliver financing promptly, at scale, and at reasonable cost, so that no developing country is forced to choose between servicing its debt and investing in its people. Multilateral development banks must be able to mobilize funds for the green and digital transitions, so that climate migration and competition over resources do not become drivers of interstate conflict. And the World Health Organization’s Pandemic Agreement must be finalized and put into force to ensure that all countries will be able to access vaccines and treatments when the next global health emergency strikes.

In a recent development, this is why Spain has sought to place development at the heart of its foreign policy. The Spanish government has championed the UN’s Sustainable Development Goals for 2030, and last year the city of Seville hosted the Fourth International Conference on Financing for Development, where delegates committed to easing the debt burden of vulnerable countries and unlocking investment for sustainable development. Spain has also promoted initiatives such as the Global Hub on Debt for Development Swaps, launched with the World Bank; the multilateral Debt Suspension Clause Alliance, which allows vulnerable countries to pause debt payments after disasters; and its own mechanism to provide up to 60 million euros in debt relief for developing countries each year. In addition, Spain has backed climate finance, global health, gender equality, food security, and social protection initiatives in partnership with multilateral institutions and international organizations. These development policies are peacebuilding policies, too.

Sources indicate that A larger project to rally the world behind legal norms and genuine multilateralism may seem unrealistic. But we have seen what happens when the normalization of war drags humanity into hell. The men and women who emerged from the ruins of World War II, the darkest chapter in human history, found a way to construct a multilateral world order. The question before our generation is whether we will preserve the rule of law or allow a return to rule by force. Whether we build the world of tomorrow through foresight and cooperation, or through the chaos and pain of another world war. We must choose wisely while the choice is still ours to make.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

It has been revealed that the highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and new U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business.

Welcome to Foreign Policy’s Southeast Asia Brief.

The highlights this week: What the ICJ’s genocide ruling means for Myanmar, a flurry of trade deals in the region, and upcoming U.S. chip controls threatening Malaysian and Thai business.

ICJ: Myanmar Committed Genocide.

The state of Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya in 2017, the International Court of Justice (ICJ), the main judicial arm of the United Nations, ruled last Thursday.

Industry observers note that the ruling documents how, following attacks by the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA), Myanmar carried out a campaign of genocidal violence against the Rohingya. It estimates that 10,000 Rohingya, about 1.2 percent of the total population, were killed.

The court ruled 9-6 that the “only reasonable inference” was that this violence revealed genocidal intent to destroy the Rohingya as a group—not just drive them out of Myanmar or exact collective punishment.

The ruling orders Myanmar to cease violence against the group and prosecute those responsible, allow the safe return of Rohingya to their homes, and pay compensation.

Sources indicate that sadly, none of this is likely. The junta has rejected the judgment as “unfair.”.

Meanwhile, another armed group called the Arakan Army, which controls most of Rakhine province and mainly represents ethnic Rakhine Buddhists, has also committed large-scale violence against the Rohingya. Fighting between the Arakan Army and Rohingya militant groups—which has seen the Rohingya militants, including the ARSA, occasionally cooperate with the junta—has added to the hostility.

The Arakan Army has made some overtures to Muslim communities in the province.

For now, though, the Arakan Army is taking a wait-and-see attitude to the ICJ judgment. A spokesperson told local media, “We are constantly monitoring the current developments. We will stand firmly on truth and justice and take appropriate action for the benefit of the Arakan region.”.

The country’s National Unity Government (NUG)—representing the civilian government overthrown by the junta in 2021 and associated with some of the main rebel forces—endorsed the judgment.

Sources indicate that this was not a given. When Aung San Suu Kyi, an icon of the NUG, was acting as the country’s de facto leader, Myanmar consistently denied that the military’s actions against the Rohingya constituted a genocide.

Recent findings suggest that in opposition, the NUG may now find its position easier. Its statement focused heavily on the junta’s culpability.

It has been revealed that but it may find the whole judgment hard to accept. The ruling finds the state of Myanmar—not just the military—guilty of genocide. And at that time when the most severe offense took place, in 2016 and 2017, the paramount power in the state apparatus was Aung San Suu Kyi.

In Southeast Asia, could this be a stumbling block for junta leader Min Aung Hlang’s push for diplomatic normalization with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN)?

Thailand—the most vocal advocate for Myanmar’s full readmission to ASEAN—looks unmoved. “Thailand must take the position that best serves the country,” Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters.

Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow argued that Thailand’s engagement did not contradict the ruling, as Thailand’s aim was to curb the current violence.

Meanwhile, two other countries—Malaysia and the Philippines—have issued official statements on the matter.

Malaysia’s brief statement mentioned that it “respects the judgment.” The Philippines’ statement seemed a shade weaker, saying it “acknowledges the judgment” and, unlike Malaysia, does not mention the Rohingya by name.

Other ASEAN countries have yet to make official statements.

Still, for countries opposed to Myanmar’s full readmission to the bloc—most notably Singapore, which serves as the ASEAN chair next year—the judgment will reinforce this skepticism.

Industry observers note that on the global stage, China has objected. “China has concerns over complications such as overreach of jurisdiction and expansive interpretation, and believes such practices are not conducive to dispute resolution,” a spokesperson stated.

In a recent development, regarding the United States, this judgment—plus the results of the country’s midterms—will likely impede the U.S. push toward normalization.

Parts of the American right reject the judgment. While the U.S. government declared in 2022that the anti-Rohingya violence constituted a genocide, some on the right are concerned that the ICJ judgments lay the groundwork for a finding of genocide against Israel, linked to its war in Gaza.

And the Myanmar junta clearly still thinks that it might find a sympathetic ear from the Trump administration.

When objecting to the ICJ ruling, a spokesperson for the Myanmar military cited a recent joint statement by U.S. President Donald Trump, Chinese President Xi Jinping, and Russian President Vladimir Putin that the International Criminal Court “must not abuse” its jurisdiction.

While the International Criminal Court is distinct from the ICJ, the spokesperson for Ming Aung Hlaing drew a parallel.

In a recent development, trump deals details. On Thursday evening, the White House disclosed the details of some of the various deals struck at last week’s ASEAN summit.

The ASEAN deals, worth a total of $17 billion, include a $12 billion sale of Boeing aircraft to Philippine Airlines.

The United States is also looking at providing $2 billion in loans for Philippine defense purchases and $400 million in military financing (though much of the funding was already committed).

Thailand will also purchase $123 million of High Mobility Artillery Rocket Systems (HIMARS) from the United States.

The terms of the Thai deal, which are not yet final, are already provoking opposition there. Many in the agricultural powerhouse are unhappy with the prospect of more agricultural imports from the United States—in particular, pork. The government is on the defense, saying that it’s the best deal it could get.

Amid controversy over the price tag, Thailand has also insisted that the HIMARS purchase is unrelated to the trade deal and was driven by national security considerations.

The Malaysian government also announced that a U.S. consortium will help develop a sovereign artificial intelligence cloud for the Malaysian government, with the United States offering $50 million in support.

In a recent development, EU-Indonesia trade deal. On Saturday, the European Union and Indonesia signed a trade deal that was 10 years in the making.

It has been revealed that under the terms of the deal, both sides will remove import duties on about 90 percent of products, including EU automotives and most agricultural exports. The products not included will see their tariffs gradually reduced or receive tariff-free quotas.

Industry observers note that indonesia expects that clothing, footwear, and palm oil will receive the biggest export boosts. It also hopes that the deal will boost European investment in Indonesia in sectors such as critical minerals, batteries, electric vehicles, pharmaceuticals, and electronics.

The deal also addresses a substantial number of nontariff barriers that often bedevil foreign products entering Indonesia.

It has been revealed that the EU’s rules on deforestation, long a sticking point for Indonesia, have been finessed. While Indonesia did not secure an exemption, the EU left the door open to accepting Indonesia’s domestic standards.

The deal comes as both the EU and Indonesia are looking to expand their global trade partnerships to offset U.S. tariffs.

Even more deals. The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China last week also saw a flurry of dealmaking.

Singaporean Prime Minister Lawrence Wong and Xi met and confirmed negotiations to upgrade the two country’s free trade agreement.

Indonesia and China mentioned they will launch formal negotiations for a comprehensive economic partnership.

They also declared strategic partnerships worth $71.8 billion, including the development of 10 “smart cities” by a partnership between Indonesian state-asset fund Danantara and a Chinese state-owned enterprise as well as deals involving a Chinese appliance maker and a consortium of other Chinese organizations investing $20 billion, also in partnership with Danantara.

Meanwhile, Vietnam revealed intends to deepen energy cooperation with Russia in both fossil fuels and nuclear energy.
