Spain holds elections this weekend—and under normal circumstances, Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez would be cruising to victory. First elected in 2018, Sánchez has established himself as Europe’s longest-serving social democratic leader. He has made Spain the best-performing economy in the European Union. His willingness to welcome immigrants, challenge U.S. President Donald Trump, and describe Israel’s military campaign in Gaza as a genocide have also turned him into an icon of the international left.

But Sánchez’s standing at home has eroded significantly in recent years. His government is mired in corruption scandals, his blanket amnesty for separatists involved in Catalonia’s illegal 2017 independence referendum has alienated many voters, and his initiative to offer a pathway to citizenship to more than 500,000 undocumented immigrants has provoked a right-wing backlash. After more than eight years in office, he is also confronting considerable voter fatigue.

Now, a worsening housing crisis is threatening to become another political liability for Sánchez. Yet he also sees it as an opportunity: By making housing the defining concern of the election, he may be able to divert attention from his political vulnerabilities while mobilizing the left-wing voters he needs to remain in power.

Last month, Sánchez dissolved parliament and called a snap election for Nov. 29, roughly seven months ahead of schedule. His biggest electoral challenge is not defeating a surging right but mobilizing left-wing voters. If Spain’s center-right and far-right opposition parties take control of the government, it will likely be because many left-wing voters stay home. An estimated 1.4 million left-wing voters are expected to sit out the elections, according to polling.

That’s what happened in another snap election called by Sánchez in 2023. That year, despite losing the popular vote to the center-right People’s Party (PP), Sánchez and his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) managed to remain in power through skillful coalition-building with separatist parties from Catalonia.

The statistics behind Spain’s housing crisis are eye-popping. Between 2015 and 2025, average home prices rose by 80 percent, while rents climbed 87 percent. Nominal wages, by contrast, increased by just 30 percent. An estimated 40 percent of Spanish renters spend an average of 40 percent of their after-tax income on rent and utilities. The burden is even heavier for young people and lower-income households. According to the Bank of Spain, the country at the moment faces a housing deficit of approximately 750,000 homes, a structural supply gap that could exceed 1 million homes by 2028.

Spain’s housing crisis has its roots in the 2008 financial collapse, when the burst of a speculative property bubble made the country an epicenter of a global crisis that also engulfed the United States. That year, Spain experienced the steepest decline in construction activity of any EU country, and newly introduced building virtually ground to a halt. Banks also tightened mortgage lending. The resulting financial crisis, which lasted from 2008 to 2013, brought down thousands of businesses—particularly banks—and pushed unemployment to 25 percent. In 2012, a $124 billion EU-backed rescue package restructured and recapitalized Spain’s financial system.

Efforts to revive the economy had the unintended consequence of exacerbating the housing crisis. One example is the residence-by-investment program, known as the golden visa. Introduced in 2013, the program sought to attract overseas investment by relaxing restrictions on foreign purchases of Spanish property. It granted Spanish residency to anyone acquiring real estate valued at a minimum of $550,000, or depositing $1.1 million in a Spanish bank.

In a recent development, foreign property purchases surged, fueled by Chinese and Russian investors. But much of the investment flowed into areas where housing was already scarce and expensive: the urban centers of Barcelona and Madrid; the coastal areas of Andalusia, Catalonia, and Valencia; and the Balearic and Canary Islands. In these markets, an influx of foreign capital contributed to rising property prices, putting homeownership increasingly out of reach for locals. Responding to public pressure, the Sánchez government abolished the program last year.

In a recent development, spain’s efforts to promote tourism have also been a mixed blessing. In 2024, the country welcomed a record 94 million international visitors, making it the world’s second-most-visited destination after France. Tourism now contributes $220 billion to the Spanish economy, accounting for 12.6 percent of GDP. But in many cities, the tourism boom has transformed entire neighborhoods into overcrowded tourist zones that overwhelm and alienate locals.

Tourism has also increased demand for foreign workers. According to the Elcano Royal Institute, Spain’s immigrant population stands at 9 million, with approximately 600,000 people arriving annually since the end of the COVID-19 pandemic. Many newcomers compete for low-rent apartments that have traditionally been available to young people and longtime residents. Elcano data also reveals that young Spaniards leave their parental homes and begin to establish independent households at an average age of 30.3, four years later than the EU average. More than 80 percent of Spaniards aged 16 to 29 still live with their parents, compared with an EU average of 68 percent.

For several years, the housing crisis has been convulsing Spanish politics, making the country home to Europe’s most vocal anti-tourism movement. In Barcelona, activists have even sprayed tourists with water guns. City officials have responded with sweeping measures to curb tourism, including some of Europe’s highest tourist taxes, a moratorium on new hotel construction, and a ban on Airbnb-style short-term rentals scheduled to take effect in 2028. But efforts to rein in tourism have set regional and local governments against federal officials in Madrid, who continue to promote tourism expansion by increasing capacity at Spanish airports.

It was an unexpected human tragedy, however, that propelled the housing crisis to the top of Sánchez’s agenda—and helped set the stage for next week’s election. On Sept. 23, police evicted ​Maricarmen Abascal, an 87-year-old disabled woman, from the Madrid apartment she had called home for 70 years. Urbagestión, the investment firm that purchased her building in 2018 from a real estate firm, had sought to raise her rent by 230 percent. When she refused to leave, authorities removed her on a stretcher. Her eviction sparked a wave of protests that culminated in hundreds of housing activists occupying Madrid’s central square. Maricarmen died on Oct. 7.

According to recent reports, shortly after her eviction, the Congress of Deputies rejected a PSOE-backed bill that would have introduced rent caps and restrictions on corporate property purchases. The legislation faced stiff opposition from conservative parties, including Junts, a Catalan separatist party that nominally supports Sánchez. Opponents argued that the proposed restrictions would further constrain housing supply. Earlier this month, responding to popular pressure, Spain’s interim parliament passed a separate housing bill aimed at limiting evictions and curbing real estate speculation. The PP opposed the legislation and pledged to repeal it if elected.

Recent findings suggest that confident that he will soon be in power, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo welcomed Sánchez’s call for early elections. Polls show a statistical dead heat between the PSOE and the PP. But because neither party is expected to win enough seats to control the Congress of Deputies outright, the far-right Vox—currently Spain’s third-largest party—could emerge as kingmaker. A PP-Vox coalition appears to be a likely outcome of the post-election negotiations. This partnership is not novel: It has been in place at the regional level since 2022 in four autonomous communities: Castilla y León, Aragón, Extremadura, and Andalusia. Vox has used regional governments to advance a nationalist and socially conservative agenda.

Sources indicate that yet the PP might be walking into a trap of its own making. As in 2023, a snap election is giving Sánchez another opportunity to demonstrate his mastery of the political comeback. Polls that year also predicted a potential governing majority for the PP and Vox, but that outcome failed to materialize. Sánchez ultimately outmaneuvered Feijóo by assembling a governing coalition.

It has been revealed that there is a powerful political paradox here: Sánchez is politically vulnerable because of the housing crisis. After all, it was under his watch that housing evolved from a growing concern into a full-blown crisis for Spanish voters. But the opposition’s resistance to his proposed remedies may allow him to turn a political liability into a potentially powerful campaign matter.

Framing the election as a referendum on who can best address Spain’s housing woes may offer Sánchez his strongest path to reelection. Rather unexpectedly, the housing crisis has allowed him to shift the campaign’s focus away from corruption and immigration and toward an problem with the potential to mobilize young voters, renters, the elderly, and lower-income households, while also resonating deeply with his Socialist base.

Recent findings suggest that omar G. Encarnación is the Charles Flint Kellogg professor of politics at Bard College. He is the author of several books, including Spanish Politics: Democracy after Dictatorship, Democracy Without Justice in Spain: The Politics of Forgetting, and, most recently, Framing Equality: The Politics of Gay Marriage Wars.

The program allows people to receive federal tax credits for donations up to $1,700 to authorized scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs), which distribute the donated scholarship funds to eligible families to be used on private or public educational expenses, including private school tuition, tutoring services, textbooks and more.

#146539. Breaking: The Paradox of Iranian Power

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 23m • 📚 Deep Dive (4665 w)

Breaking: The Paradox of Iranian Power

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 23 min read (4665 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignaffairs

⏱️ ~23 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger.
  • Recent findings suggest that they are not entirely misguided in that belief.
  • According to recent reports, the joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why the Islamic Republic Can’t Make Peace.

Iran’s theocratic rulers have drawn a Nietzschean lesson from nearly half a century of crises: what has not killed their revolution has only made it stronger. In 2026, the Islamic Republic survived a nationwide uprising and a devastating war with the United States and Israel that eliminated its leaders, decimated its military, and ravaged its economy. Yet rather than reconsider the principles and policies that have stoked nearly five decades of confrontation, isolation, and popular unrest, Tehran’s rulers drew the opposite conclusion: revolutionary ideology was not an albatross weighing the regime down, but a life preserver keeping it afloat.

Recent findings suggest that they are not entirely misguided in that belief. Since the 1979 revolution transformed Iran from a pro-American monarchy into an anti-American theocracy, the regime’s organizing principles have been the imposition of theocratic rule at home and resistance against Israel and the United States abroad. These policies have fueled recurring internal unrest and external conflicts that have impoverished, isolated, and destabilized Iran. Paradoxically, however, revolutionary regimes that survive such challenges often emerge more resilient, cohesive, and confident in their ideological convictions. The Islamic Republic, under the new leadership of Mojtaba Khamenei, appears to be following the same pattern.

According to recent reports, the joint U.S.-Israeli war on Iran did not meaningfully rally an impoverished and abused Iranian society around its oppressive regime. It did, however, rally the regime around the revolution. Rather than embrace the possibility of a different political order, Tehran’s rulers closed ranks and extended the Khamenei era—literally, by anointing Mojtaba Khamenei to succeed his father, the slain supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei. “God’s grace is clear,” supporters chanted, “A young Khamenei is here!”.

At home, the war entrenched a revolutionary elite whose priority is resistance, not governance. That will only prolong the country’s crisis. The regime can suppress revolts but cannot address the conditions that produce them, leaving Iran trapped in a downward spiral of despotism, decline, and despair.

Sources indicate that U.S. President Donald Trump’s attempt to resolve the Iranian challenge instead exacerbated it. The war, rolled out in the midst of negotiations, has degraded Tehran’s military capabilities but hardened its revolutionary character, deepened its already profound mistrust of Washington, and taught its rulers a dangerous lesson: violence, not dialogue, secures concessions. Tehran has established upcoming precedents for attacking its neighbors, disrupting global energy supplies, and asserting control over the Strait of Hormuz. Its leaders are determined to rebuild their military capabilities and avenge Khamenei’s death, while Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from restoring the capacity to threaten it. What Tehran may regard as necessary to rebuild its deterrence, Israel may regard as preparation for another war.

Recent findings suggest that washington can choose to end its war with Iran, but it cannot end the Islamic Republic’s confrontation with the United States. Israel cannot afford to ignore an adversary it regards as an existential threat. Gulf Arab states may have little say in whether Israel and Iran fight another war, but they could bear some of its greatest costs as their cities, energy infrastructure, and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz are vulnerable to Iranian retaliation. Tehran regards the Gulf’s economic and technological achievements not as examples to emulate, but as vulnerabilities to exploit and targets to threaten. For these reasons, the end of this war is likely to prove an intermission rather than a resolution.

The challenges the Islamic Republic poses to the Middle East, the United States, and the global economy can ultimately be resolved only with political change in Tehran. Yet getting through 2026 has simply reinforced the Islamic Republic’s revolutionary conviction that its survival is best ensured through continuity, not change. The country will remain suspended between war and peace abroad, and between prolonged decay and sudden upheaval at home. Iran is thus left in a paradox. Revolutionary ideology has led the country toward destruction. But abandoning revolutionary ideology could lead the regime toward collapse.

Industry observers note that like all ailing autocracies, the Islamic Republic has the potential to both gradually atrophy or abruptly implode. Russian Tsar Nicholas I first referred to the Ottoman Empire as “the sick man” of Europe in 1853; its end came seven decades later. George Kennan wrote in these pages in 1947 that the Soviet Union “bears within it the seeds of its own decay, and that the sprouting of these seeds is well advanced.” It took another 44 years for the Soviet Union to collapse.

In a recent development, the Islamic Republic of Iran has come to resemble the Leaning Tower of Pisa: seemingly on the verge of collapse but defying political gravity decade after decade. Despite its abundant natural resources and human capital, theocratic Iran has been a case study in squandered national potential. Its economy is trapped in recurring crises, its currency is ravaged by inflation, and generations of educated citizens seek their futures abroad. Nearly half a century after the revolution, Iran’s real GDP per capita remains nearly a quarter below its 1976 peak. That means that many Iranians are materially worse off than their parents and grandparents were before the revolution, an economic regression typically suffered only by failed states or societies ravaged by civil war.

It has been revealed that while Iran’s economy has regressed, its society has progressed. Over the last five decades, its population has nearly tripled, and a predominantly rural and traditional society has become increasingly urban, educated, and socially liberal. Since the 2022–23 “Woman, Life, Freedom” protests, mandatory veiling—what Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini once called the “flag” of the Islamic Revolution—appears increasingly unenforceable. Women now routinely walk down the streets of Tehran and other cities with their hair uncovered. The breaking of this taboo will embolden Iranians to break others. In short, Iran’s citizens look forward, Iran’s rulers look backward, and Iran’s economy spirals downward. It is a country whose people have moved beyond the revolution, but whose rulers refuse to leave it behind.

In a recent development, the historian Crane Brinton compared revolutions to fevers that eventually break, ushering in a period of moderation known as Thermidor. Yet many decades after the revolution, Iran’s rulers still refuse to lower the temperature. Iranian society has long sought a return to normalcy, but the regime fears that ending the revolution would mean ending its own rule. The growing gap between rulers and the ruled can be sustained only through continued brutality. The Islamic Republic’s aspiring Deng Xiaopings were sidelined for fear they might become the regime’s Mikhail Gorbachevs. Its Vaclav Havels have been imprisoned, exiled, or killed. Edmund Burke warned that “a state without the means of some change is without the means of its conservation.” Yet the Islamic Republic’s rulers appear more willing to risk breaking the regime than to allow themselves to bend, and more willing to risk another calamitous war than to abandon the revolutionary principles that have sustained their power.

Revolutionary regimes are surprisingly resilient. As the political scientists Steven Levitsky and Lucan Way write in Revolution and Dictatorship, such regimes tend to last nearly three times as long as their nonrevolutionary counterparts, despite being twice as likely to be involved in wars. Although their radicalism often triggers counterrevolution or external war, regimes that survive those early challenges commonly develop three pillars of durability: “a cohesive ruling elite,” “a highly developed and loyal coercive apparatus,” and “the destruction of rival organizations and alternative centers of power in society.”.

It has been revealed that the Islamic Republic has developed these three pillars because of, not in spite of, decades of internal opposition and near-constant hot and cold wars. The 444-day seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran beginning in 1979 and the eight-year war with Saddam Hussein’s Iraq, which began the following year, were foundational crises that brought international isolation and economic devastation to Iran but helped entrench Khomeini’s theocracy. Both were prolonged well beyond their initial objectives, in part because they served the regime’s internal consolidation: the hostage crisis marginalized moderates, while the exigencies of the war with Iraq smothered internal dissent and helped build the military-industrial system—namely the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC)—to entrench theocratic government. Just as the Long March forged the bonds and credentials of China’s revolutionary elite in the 1930s, the Iran-Iraq War of the 1980s forged those of the Revolutionary Guard commanders who rule Iran today.

It has been revealed that whereas most states seek normalcy and the resolution of crises, crises in the Islamic Republic provided fertile soil for the revolution. As Abolhassan Bani-Sadr, the Islamic Republic’s first president, observed in 2003, after more than two decades in exile: “With the end of the war, crisis-making did not end. The mullahs’ regime, which was born of crisis-making, could not continue its life without making crises.” The Islamic Republic has made disequilibrium its equilibrium. Indeed, some within the regime privately believe that IRGC attacks on shipping during this year’s cease-fire, as well as the maximalist demands of Iranian negotiators, were meant to prolong the war and entrench the power of hard-liners, much as the Iran-Iraq War helped cement their position.

Industry observers note that by attacking Iran weeks after the regime killed thousands of protesters, one of the bloodiest massacres in modern Iranian history, Trump provided Tehran with an external crisis to divert attention from its internal one. Imagine if the United States had attacked the Soviet Union in 1982, as its economy stagnated, its ideology languished, and its aging rulers struggled to preserve a discredited political order. Rather than hastening communism’s demise, such an attack might have revitalized its defenders, discredited its critics, and transformed a crisis of legitimacy into a struggle for national survival. Something similar seems to have happened in Iran. The war allowed Tehran’s rulers to portray their decades of hostility toward the United States not as the source of Iran’s predicament, but as vindication of their worldview. It is telling that while Israeli and U.S. forces have killed many of the regime’s top political and military leaders, no high-level officials have defected.

It has been revealed that no one in today’s Islamic Republic has the stature to push for reform or rapprochement with Washington; its many veto men, whose privileges depend on the status quo, have the power to block both. Profound change requires consensus. Inertia can be entrenched by a few.

Recent findings suggest that A great deal depends on the largely invisible Mojtaba Khamenei. It remains to be seen for how long the Islamic Republic’s political and military elite will defer to a supreme leader who has, for whatever reason, withdrawn from public view. Iranian political culture tends toward personality cults, and over much of the last century the country has largely been led by four strongmen: Reza Shah (1925 to 1941), Mohammad Reza Shah Pahlavi (1941 to 1979), Khomeini (1979 to 1989), and Ali Khamenei (1989 to 2026). Few major countries have experienced such extraordinary continuity of personal rule across radically different political systems. The present situation—an absent supreme leader hidden from public view, possibly for health reasons or out of fear of assassination, and competing centers of power within the security establishment—therefore looks like an unstable equilibrium.

According to recent reports, after Khomeini came to power, in 1979, outside observers commonly assumed Iran’s revolutionary fervor would fade and that the country’s fresh leaders could be won over with the right mix of respect and economic inducements. “Khomeini will be somewhat of a saint when we get over the panic,” Andrew Young, a UN ambassador in the Carter administration, predicted in February 1979. “In two years, our relations with Iran will be on a pretty even keel.” But today, the regime still chants “Death to America.” Governments do not cling to policies that they believe endanger their survival. The enduring mistake has been to assume that Iran’s leaders cannot possibly mean what they repeatedly say.

The Islamic Republic has always framed its conflict with the United States not merely as a geopolitical dispute but also as a moral and ideological struggle. Khomeini, who outlined his vision of Islamic government nearly a decade before the revolution and implemented it after seizing power, called the United States “the foremost enemy of Islam” in his last will and testament. His successor, Ali Khamenei, maintained remarkable ideological consistency over nearly four decades, repeatedly describing the rivalry as an “inherent conflict—an inherent incompatibility.” For both men, their publicly articulated convictions proved a far more reliable guide to the Islamic Republic’s conduct than the reassurances of its diplomats or the wishful interpretations of Western observers.

Khamenei’s son and successor Mojtaba—whose face and voice have not been seen or heard since he became supreme leader in March 2026—has echoed his father in his public pronouncements. “The criminal rulers of America and the illegitimate Zionist regime,” he mentioned in one statement, “are not merely enemies of the Islamic Republic, Iran, or the vast front of Islamic resistance; they harbor enmity toward the entire Islamic ummah”—the Muslim community. After the Democratic victories in the U.S. midterm elections in November, a post on Mojtaba Khamenei’s official English-language X account proclaimed that “the process of the US’s collapse has accelerated.” He further warned that neither American elections nor Iranian concessions would alter the “hegemonic system” of the United States and its hostility toward the Islamic Republic.

The elder Khamenei’s assassination at the start of the war continued the transformation of Iran from a country led by clerics into one dominated by current and former IRGC officers. Many observers assumed this shift from turbans to uniforms would move the regime’s focus from religious ideology to national interest. This has yet to happen. Although the regime has adopted more overtly nationalist rhetoric, it still subordinates the welfare and security of Iranians to the goals of the revolution. The motivations of security officials may be more financial than theological, but their interests have remained bound to the same revolutionary order.

Siamak Namazi, an Iranian American who spent nearly eight years as a hostage of the IRGC in Tehran’s Evin prison, describes the Islamic Republic as a “competitive kleptocracy masquerading as a theocracy.” Many of the regime’s elite, he has observed, are driven less by religious dogma than by the spoils of power: preferential exchange rates, privileged loans, import licenses, and a cut of the smuggling trade. “The revolutionary Kool-Aid,” he remarked, “is reserved for the ranks, because someone still has to believe enough to open fire on their own countrymen.” The true believers also have a great deal to lose. A January 2026 Bloomberg report alleged that Mojtaba Khamenei had used a middleman to build a financial empire in the West, including $138 million in British luxury real estate and Swiss bank accounts.

It has been revealed that the IRGC has eclipsed the clergy in both political and economic power, with some estimates suggesting they control more than a third of Iran’s economy. Individual commanders have accumulated fortunes, often by enabling the business activities of their children, known as aghazadehs, or princelings. Yet rather than challenge the supreme leader, the senior command’s public statements suggest continued solidarity with the office. Mohsen Rezaei, a longtime IRGC commander with substantial family business interests who returned to serve as secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, expressed his devotion to Mojtaba in a September 2026 interview with state television. “Let us preserve our unity,” he insisted. “Let us preserve our dignity. Let us march behind the leader of the revolution.”.

According to recent reports, in a 26-page open letter to the American people published the same month, the IRGC declared that the war had “reinvigorated the Islamic Republic” and would ensure the regime’s survival for decades. Rather than question the ideology that had brought Iran to this precipice, the corps reaffirmed velayat-e faqih, the doctrine of clerical guardianship, as an “embodiment of all godly virtues in the political sphere” that empowered Iran to stand firm against diabolical powers. Revolutionary and religious dogma were not the source of Iran’s predicament, they concluded, but rather the “main factors underpinning Iran’s victory.”.

Iran’s rulers are neither pragmatic nationalists guided by traditional state interests nor an apocalyptic death cult. They outsource the politics of martyrdom to regional militias while ruthlessly practicing the politics of survival at home. For the true believers, abandoning the revolution would mean betraying their convictions; for its profiteers, it would mean jeopardizing their power and privileges. When the regime’s survival is at stake, they may change their tactics, but they won’t change their worldview.

The war has left Tehran both weaker and much more aggressive. Before the war, the Islamic Republic resembled a zombie regime: its ideology, legitimacy, and its 86-year-old supreme leader all appeared to be fading. Since the outbreak of the war, it has come to resemble a gangster regime—one that practices extortion as statecraft—and is emboldened to attack its neighbors, the global economy, and the United States to extract concessions.

According to recent reports, tehran has been rewarded for its defiance by Trump. In his dramatic address launching the war in February 2026, Trump vowed to end Iran’s nuclear weapons ambitions, destroy its missile capabilities, and neutralize its regional proxies. He encouraged Iranians to overthrow their “wicked” dictatorship. But the president soon changed his tune. Although Trump believed the war would be a swift “little excursion,” Iran’s attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz and its over 6,700 missile and drone attacks on its Gulf neighbors compelled him to attempt one of the most striking reversals in modern American foreign policy.

In a recent development, in June, Trump signed a memorandum of understanding with Tehran that gave away the store. He pledged to lift all sanctions as part of a final agreement, release frozen Iranian assets, permit Iranian oil exports, and work with regional partners on a $300 billion reconstruction package. The agreement also accepted an Iranian role in determining the future administration of the Strait of Hormuz, committed Washington to noninterference in Iran’s internal affairs, and made no mention of Iran’s missiles or regional proxies.

According to recent reports, in just four months, Trump had gone from pursuing the most hawkish Iran policy ever to offering the most generous diplomatic terms since the 1979 revolution. A policy of regime change became one of accommodation. Although the memorandum of understanding was short-lived—each side blames the other for abrogating it—the lesson Tehran learned was unmistakable: restraint projects weakness, whereas aggression is rewarded.

Recent findings suggest that “We seize concessions not through dialogue, but with missiles,” declared Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, a former IRGC commander, the current speaker of the parliament, and one of the regime’s most powerful figures. “The winner of any agreement,” he added, “is the one who is better prepared for war from the day after.” Tehran is already signaling that its chief postwar priority will not be to rebuild its decimated economy, but to restore—and expand—its ability to impose costs on its adversaries.

Recent findings suggest that the Strait of Hormuz offers the clearest example of this dynamic. What was once an Iranian threat has become, in Tehran’s eyes, an entitlement: the ability to regulate passage through one of the world’s most consequential energy chokepoints. For Iran, this constitutes both economic leverage and a potential deterrent against future attacks on itself and its regional proxies. For the rest of the world, it creates the prospect that Tehran can hold global energy markets hostage whenever it chooses.

Sources indicate that before the war, the Iranian regime’s longtime ambitions to drive the United States from the Middle East and end Israel’s existence appeared fanciful. Today, the growing number of American politicians and commentators who have called for the United States to end its aid to Israel and wind down its regional military presence has emboldened Tehran to believe it is winning the ideological war. “POTUS clearly recognizes that the vast majority of Americans are disgusted with Israel,” Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said in a post on social media in November. He continued: “Americans are evidently sick and tired of Israel bamboozling US administrations into Forever Wars. They had enough. So has our region.”.

The Islamic Republic’s newfound confidence is partly rooted in its ability to inflict enormous damage at comparatively little cost. Its Persian Gulf neighbors have spent decades and trillions of dollars transforming themselves into global hubs of energy, transportation, finance, and technology. And Iran can now threaten all of it with cheap Shahed drones against which the United States and its partners must field multimillion-dollar interceptors—a costly undertaking that Nick Carter, a retired British general and former chief of the British defense staff, likened to “Ferraris being thrown at Frisbees.” Building is costly and slow; destruction is fast and cheap. Rezaei has pledged to target undersea cables, data centers, and artificial intelligence facilities across the Gulf in the event of renewed fighting.

The Islamic Republic’s theory of victory does not require defeating the United States militarily. It only requires persuading two audiences—the American public and Iran’s Gulf neighbors—that the U.S. military presence in the region and the partnership with Israel bring more harm than good. The attacks on American bases, Gulf data centers, and ships passing through the Strait of Hormuz are a message that the road to regional security must go through Iran, not the United States or Israel. “The nations and territories of the region will no longer serve as a shield for American bases,” Mojtaba Khamenei has declared.

But this Iranian aggression is likely to produce the opposite of what it intends. Tehran’s threats against the Gulf only stoke the anxieties that sustain Washington’s military presence in the region. The result is a self-perpetuating cycle in which Gulf governments seek American protection against Iran, Tehran attempts to evict Washington from the region, and each new round of conflict deepens the Gulf states’ dependence on the United States.

Iran’s confrontation with Israel poses a different, potentially more explosive danger. The regime’s hostility to Israel has survived the destruction of much of Tehran’s military infrastructure and its regional proxy network. Iranian leaders remain determined to rebuild their missile and drone arsenals, restore the capabilities of allies such as Hezbollah, and avenge the killing of Ali Khamenei. Yet Israel is equally determined to prevent Iran from reconstituting the capabilities that threatened it before the war. Each side may therefore interpret the other’s attempts at deterrence as preparations for another attack.

It has been revealed that as for Trump’s original justification for the war—to avert an Iranian nuclear bomb—his actions and words have persuaded a growing number of Iranian officials to openly advocate nuclear arms development. The president himself supplied Tehran’s talking points. “If they had a nuclear weapon,” Trump told a crowd of supporters six months into the war, “I’d be calling the supreme leader and I’d be saying: ‘Mr. Supreme Leader, how are you, sir? Is there anything we can do for you?’—as opposed to bombing the crap out of him.”.

Since the 1979 revolution, Washington has tended to underestimate the Islamic Republic’s agency and overestimate its own ability to shape Iran’s future. Advocates of engagement often blame American hostility for Tehran’s intransigence, while advocates of confrontation have blamed American weakness. One side has overestimated the Islamic Republic’s flexibility; the other, its fragility. Both have been susceptible to what the former U.S. national security adviser H. R. McMaster has called “strategic narcissism”: the assumption that adversaries are primarily reacting to the United States rather than acting on their own interests, identities, and ambitions.

Trump’s war exposed the limits of trying both to bomb Iran into submission and to bribe it into moderation. In the span of four months, Washington employed overwhelming military force to weaken or overthrow the Islamic Republic, then offered sweeping economic and diplomatic incentives to alter its behavior. Neither altered a revolutionary stance that has been remarkably consistent for decades. As Henry Kissinger wrote in 1957, “The distinguishing feature of a revolutionary power is not that it feels threatened . . . but that nothing can reassure it.”.

The seeds of the next war have already been planted. Regardless of what the United States chooses to do, the Islamic Republic’s renewed confidence, along with its resolve to rebuild its military might and retaliate for the death of its supreme leader, portends another showdown with Israel. Each side now views the other as an existential threat, and there is no direct channel of dialogue to prevent miscalculation and a potentially even more destructive war. For Washington, the implication is clear: The United States may seek to disengage from the Middle East, but it cannot insulate itself from the consequences of another war between Iran and Israel.

The Islamic Republic’s most consequential compromises came in 1988, when Khomeini reluctantly accepted a cease-fire ending the eight-year war with Iraq, and in 2015, when Iran agreed to stringent restrictions on its nuclear program. Although separated by nearly three decades, both decisions followed a similar logic. Faced with overwhelming pressure, international isolation, and a diplomatic off-ramp that does not require it to change its identity, the Islamic Republic has demonstrated a capacity to make concessions—but only in the service of living to fight another day.

According to recent reports, in a 2013 speech foreshadowing Tehran’s nuclear compromise, Ali Khamenei described this approach as “heroic flexibility.” The supreme leader likened the regime to a wrestler who “highlights flexibility for technical reasons” but must never “forget who his opponent is and what he is doing.” Tactical flexibility, Khamenei insisted, must never come at the expense of Iran’s “revolutionary nature”: “The fact that the world has changed cannot give us an excuse to change our behavior, our ideals, and our goals.” Ali Khamenei had the legitimacy to push for heroic flexibility. The current regime is filled with men who will pursue escalation long before they ever call for compromise.

Sources indicate that today, the challenges posed by Iran are much greater than a decade ago. Washington must not only prevent it from acquiring nuclear weapons but also deter it from attacking its neighbors, disrupting the global energy trade through the Strait of Hormuz, and waging AI-assisted cyberwarfare and influence operations against the United States and its partners. At the same time, Washington has fewer allies and less diplomatic leverage than it did in 2015, and the trust gap between the two governments may prove unbridgeable. The Iranian regime believes that global public opinion is on its side, not Trump’s.

Sources indicate that the 48-year history of U.S. policy toward the Islamic Republic shows that grand designs, whether for regime change or rapprochement, have failed. On two occasions, in 1988 and 2015, both sides reached narrow agreements that addressed Tehran’s conduct rather than its character. Lasting change, however, can come only from within Iran, when the pillars that sustain the Islamic Republic—a cohesive elite, a loyal coercive apparatus, and the absence of rival centers of power—crack. Rather than widening those cracks, Trump’s war may have narrowed them.

Iran’s rulers see the regime’s survival as proof of their own strength. Yet each crisis they weather leaves the country poorer, its people more estranged, and the regime more dependent on brutality to endure. Like Washington before it, Tehran now overestimates what force can achieve; its hubris may help produce the next war, just as the repression that quelled the last uprising will invariably fuel another. The revolutionary ideology that keeps the regime afloat will continue to weigh Iran down, leaving in place a leadership even more intent on resisting its adversaries, at home and abroad, than on governing its people. The regime may declare victory, but for the proud people of Iran—an ancient civilization and an energy superpower with a worthless currency, a shunned passport, and a leader in hiding—there is little reason to celebrate. What has not killed the Islamic Republic is slowly killing Iran.

KARIM SADJADPOUR is a Senior Fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace.

Industry observers note that ES Foundry, a U.S. manufacturer of high-efficiency solar cells, is at RE+ 2026 this week to showcase its American-made solar cells and announce a milestone in its operating capacity.

According to the tech giant, it is the first and only crystalline silicon solar cell manufacturer to ship more than 1 gigawatt (GW) of domestically manufactured solar cells in the United States.

As one of the few U.S. solar cell manufacturers with a fully operational facility producing and shipping cells to customers, ES Foundry is helping move American solar manufacturing to commercial reality.

Recent findings suggest that in July, the manufacturer confirmed it reached its full 3-GW manufacturing capacity. The company began production on its first 1-GW line last year and has now completed its 2-GW expansion line.

Solar Power World attended the opening of its Greenwood, South Carolina facility last year, reporting on its manufacturing outfit and its unique approach to supply deals that include working with large-scale project developers and utilities to guarantee domestic content supplies.

At RE+, attendees can see its U.S.-manufactured high-efficiency monocrystalline bifacial PERC solar cells and meet with organization representatives to discuss domestic sourcing, manufacturing capabilities, and the evolving needs of the U.S. solar market.

According to recent reports, “There’s an important difference between talking about building a domestic solar supply chain and actually making it happen,” mentioned ES Foundry CEO Alex Zhu in a statement. “At ES Foundry, we’re manufacturing at commercial scale, shipping cells to customers and navigating the realities of U.S. production every day. That experience gives us a unique perspective on what it will take to build a competitive, sustainable American solar industry. Success requires more than manufacturing capacity. It requires the right economics, technology investments, customer demand and policies to support long-term growth. We’re proud to be delivering on the promise of American manufacturing today while helping shape the industry’s future.”.

Visit ES Foundry at RE+ 2026: Booth C7434, November 16–19, Las Vegas, Nevada.

Europe’s Economic Sovereignty Is All Talk and Little Action

  • Nearly 25 years after the euro began circulating, one might assume that it is the go-to currency for European Union firms doing business outside the bloc.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Get audio access with any FP subscription.

European debates about economic security often sound like a succession of buzzwords: “strategic autonomy,” “de-risking,” “diversification.” For all the lofty aspirations, none of these policies have done much to change Europe’s trajectory. As the European Council on Foreign Relations’ new report on global interdependence (which I co-authored) documents, the European Union keeps growing more reliant on the United States in finance, technology, and trade.

Let’s start with finance. Nearly 25 years after the euro began circulating, one might assume that it is the go-to currency for European Union firms doing business outside the bloc. The data tells a different story: In 2024, EU firms used the euro for only 46 percent of their transactions outside the EU, down just 2 percentage points from 2016, compared to a steady 41 percent invoiced in dollars. Despite long-standing calls from the European Commission for companies to switch to euros, the dollar’s prominence partly reflects its dominance of energy markets; in 2024, EU firms used dollars for 87 percent of their petroleum imports.

European debates about economic security often sound like a succession of buzzwords: “strategic autonomy,” “de-risking,” “diversification.” For all the lofty aspirations, none of these policies have done much to change Europe’s trajectory. As the European Council on Foreign Relations’ new report on global interdependence (which I co-authored) documents, the European Union keeps growing more reliant on the United States in finance, technology, and trade.

Sources indicate that let’s start with finance. Nearly 25 years after the euro began circulating, one might assume that it is the go-to currency for European Union firms doing business outside the bloc. The data tells a different story: In 2024, EU firms used the euro for only 46 percent of their transactions outside the EU, down just 2 percentage points from 2016, compared to a steady 41 percent invoiced in dollars. Despite long-standing calls from the European Commission for companies to switch to euros, the dollar’s prominence partly reflects its dominance of energy markets; in 2024, EU firms used dollars for 87 percent of their petroleum imports.

According to recent reports, next, look at European financial investments. Since U.S. President Donald Trump embraced tariffs in 2025 and then threatened to seize Greenland in early 2026, there has been talk in some EU capitals that divesting Europe’s significant holdings of U.S. Treasurys could be a way to pressure Washington. EU-based investment funds and central banks must have missed the memo: Together, they made net purchases of U.S. Treasurys totaling $56 billion between January 2025 and this August. (The data excludes Belgium, Ireland, and Luxembourg, as these countries’ hefty holdings mostly reflect their role as financial hubs.).

Recent findings suggest that despite Paris’s role as Europe’s vocal champion of strategic autonomy, French investors accounted for 61 percent of these purchases—cementing France’s status as the top EU holder of U.S. Treasurys, with $363 billion in holdings as of August.

EU appetite for U.S. public debt stems from one simple fact: At just $7 trillion, the combined stock of German, French, and EU-issued sovereign bonds is five times smaller than the stock of U.S. Treasurys. Without a greater supply of euro-denominated safe assets, EU funds have little choice but to accumulate U.S. Treasurys. This increases Europe’s exposure to threats from the United States, such as the advice of former Federal Reserve Board of Governors member Stephen Miran to withhold part of the interest that Washington pays on foreign-owned Treasurys.

Sources indicate that these days, all eyes are on artificial intelligence, and this sector highlights the extent to which calls for European de-risking are going unanswered in the tech field. In late October, Epoch AI ranked 64 models at or above the level of OpenAI’s GPT-5. Of these, 49 were American, 14 were Chinese, and just one was European—France’s Mistral Large 4. It’s no surprise, then, that American models are becoming the default choice for European firms. According to the German tech industry association Bitkom, 76 percent of German companies using AI rely on OpenAI’s ChatGPT, up from 70 percent last year. Not a single one of the surveyed firms uses Mistral.

Industry observers note that U.S. dominance of Western AI is unlikely to end any time soon. Epoch researchers also found that between January and June 2026, U.S.-based firms bought 78 percent of all AI semiconductors powering data centers and supporting the training of new, more powerful models. EU-based companies purchased just 5 percent of these chips during the same period, paving the way for the trans-Atlantic AI gap to widen further.

Current EU investment metrics make it hard to imagine a more positive outcome for European ambitions in other frontier sectors, such as quantum computing and biotechnology. In the field of quantum technology, data from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology demonstrates that only four EU countries (Finland, France, Germany, and the Netherlands) have funding levels worth noting. Yet together, they accounted for just around 10 percent of global financing in 2025.

In a recent development, meanwhile, the United States captured nearly two-thirds of worldwide funding for quantum technology, while Britain and Canada—both much smaller economies than the EU—are also notable players. In medical biotech, the pattern is the same: U.S. firms secured 63 percent of global venture capital between January 2015 and June 2025, nine times the 7 percent raised by EU firms, according to the European Commission.

Recent findings suggest that the abysmally low levels of funding for quantum computing and biotech suggest that current European concerns about dependence on the United States for AI are only the start of a long line of similar debates. Time and again, EU firms and consumers end up buying critical technology from elsewhere that they did not finance and develop at home. As the United States’ decision in June to cut off global access to Anthropic’s Fable 5 indicated, this gives Washington a simple way to deprive Europe of critical technology.

Trade is the final area in which the EU is reliant on the United States. Consider EU exports. Despite pledges to diversify, European firms have become more dependent on the U.S. market over the past decade. U.S. firms bought 21 percent of the EU’s goods exports in 2025, up from 17 percent in 2015. While a rush to stockpile European goods before the start of U.S. tariffs can partly explain the spike in EU exports to the United States last year, it does not change the long-term trend. Nor is this Europe rerouting exports that China no longer buys; at 8 percent in 2025, China’s share of EU goods exports was unchanged from 2015.

Industry observers note that instead, two factors help explain why European exporters have become increasingly reliant on the U.S. market. The first is pharmaceuticals. Half of the 244 billion euro rise in EU exports to the United States between 2015 and 2025 can be attributed to medicines, such as the Irish-manufactured ingredients of Eli Lilly’s blockbuster obesity drug Mounjaro. In 2025, the United States absorbed 43 percent of EU exports of drugs and medical ingredients, up from 28 percent in 2015. Booming pharmaceutical exports are good news for Europe, but shipping nearly half of them to the United States gives Washington a clear target.

The second factor is that the EU’s pledge to diversify trade ties toward middle powers is materializing only slowly. The share of EU goods exports going to 10 major middle powers, including India, Indonesia, and Turkey, remained unchanged between 2015 and 2025, at only 15 percent.

Industry observers note that in terms of imports, the EU’s reliance on the United States is growing, too—particularly in energy and intellectual property (IP). Increased dependence on U.S. energy following Europe’s shift away from Russian supplies is familiar by now: U.S. firms now supply almost two-thirds of EU imports of liquefied natural gas, up from zero in 2015. The lesser-known story has to do with IP. Contrary to Britain, Japan, and the United States, the EU is a net importer of IP, such as software, patents, or trademarks. U.S. firms supply 80 percent of these imports, and the trade is one-sided. Eurostat documents that at 213 billion euros in 2025, the bloc’s imports of U.S. IP have grown sevenfold over the past decade. Last year, the EU bought six times as much IP from the United States as vice versa.

Failed attempts to achieve strategic autonomy, de-risking, and diversification have a precedent. In 2019, Britain, France, and Germany created INSTEX, a barter mechanism intended to maintain European trade with Iran despite U.S. secondary sanctions. INSTEX handled just one transaction before closing in 2023.

Industry observers note that europe’s ambition to achieve economic security stands a better chance of succeeding if Brussels gets serious about creating a euro-denominated safe asset, investing heavily in frontier technology sectors, and doubling down on signing trade deals with middle powers. Delivering on these reforms would be a winning strategy—and not just a succession of buzzwords.

The European Council on Foreign Relations’ report, Interdependence, Revised: A Fresh Dictionary for the World Economy by Agathe Demarais and Chiara Malaponti, was released earlier this month.

Agathe Demarais is a columnist at Foreign Policy, a senior policy fellow on geoeconomics and technology at the European Council on Foreign Relations, a visiting professor at the College of Europe, a former global forecasting director at the Economist Intelligence Unit, and the author of Backfire: How Sanctions Reshape the World Against U.S. Interests. Richard Volpe, professor of agricultural economics at California Polytechnic State University, explains how higher prices for food, energy, packaging and transportation could make holiday meals harder on household budgets.

The turkey may be a holiday bargain, but rising prices for meat, dairy and fresh foods could make the rest of the Thanksgiving spread cost much more this year.

Richard Volpe, a professor of agribusiness at Cal Poly San Luis Obispo, told Fox News Digital that sustained high energy costs in the midst of the Iran war — particularly for diesel — are pushing up grocery prices just as households prepare to host holiday meals.

Surging prices of ham and eggnog, in particular, could put a damper on some holiday favorites.

Shoppers can compare prices, watch for store promotions and consider store brands to keep holiday grocery bills in check. (Kim Raff/Bloomberg/Getty Images).

Sources indicate that "Most of the biggest increases are things like fruits, vegetables and meats," Volpe noted. "Fresh and refrigerated foods feel those costs sooner than shelf-stable products.".

7 COSTCO THANKSGIVING FOOD DEALS AND STEALS THAT SHOPPERS CAN'T MISS THIS HOLIDAY SEASON.

Dairy is also especially energy and transportation intensive, putting holiday staples such as butter and eggnog under pressure.

Volpe said shoppers willing to switch brands and take advantage of store promotions can keep holiday meals more affordable.

"If you are less worried about brand or banner loyalty, and you’re able to follow promotions and look for these sort of aggressive, enticing deals, there are still ways to achieve savings and to keep those Thanksgiving and holiday dinners relatively affordable," Volpe said.

With beef and pork prices high, some households may serve turkey for other holiday meals in place of pot roast or ham. (iStock).

He also acknowledged that high beef and pork prices could contribute to some households deciding to dine on a different main dish for their holiday meals this year.

"Beef and pork are particularly expensive right now, so I would expect to see some substitutions there," he mentioned. "I would strongly suspect that across the country, there are folks who are roasting turkeys and chickens, or even salmon or some other large sort of centerpiece to the meal that’s protein-based other than beef and pork.".

AMERICANS ARE MAKING COSTLY GROCERY MISTAKE EVEN BEFORE ENTERING THE STORE, EXPERT WARNS.

Swapping the menu may help, but Volpe said skipping the grocery store for a restaurant or catered meal is unlikely to save money.

"It is still cheaper to go to the grocery store and prepare food at home," Volpe said.

Industry observers note that volpe told Fox News Digital that whole turkeys are often discounted before Thanksgiving as grocers use low prices to draw shoppers into stores. (Liz Clayman/Bloomberg/Getty Images).

He said restaurant prices have risen nearly twice as fast as grocery prices over the past two to two and a half years.

According to recent reports, "I'm not expecting food price inflation anything like what we saw in ’21 and ’22," he stated. "We’re actually still very likely on track for roughly normal food price inflation on the year.".

Emily Kilcrease is Senior Fellow and Director of the Energy, Economics, and Security Program at the Center for a New American Security. From 2019 to 2021, first in the Trump administration and then in the Biden administration, she was Deputy Assistant U.S. Trade Representative for Investment.

Vivek Chilukuri is Senior Fellow and Director of the Technology and National Security Program at the Center for a Upcoming American Security. He previously served as Legislative Director to Senator Michael Bennet and as a policy adviser at the U.S. Department of State.

Sources indicate that how China Exploited a Massive Loophole in U.S. National Security—and How Congress Can Close It.

Emily Kilcrease and Vivek Chilukuri.

Industry observers note that the reinstatement of Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia this week added another twist to a scandal that has transfixed Washington and Silicon Valley. The stakes go beyond the swings of the stock market or the salacious details about Huang’s affairs, including with Alice Huang, a former executive at the Singaporean firm Megaspeed and a potential Chinese asset. At its core, the scandal has exposed something that matters far more than any one man or firm: American export-control policy remains riddled with loopholes, hobbled by incapacity and infighting, and divorced from clear strategy. Unless Washington fixes this, it risks imperiling the United States’ hard-won advantage in artificial intelligence.

It has been revealed that this export policy failure is more than the sum of specific deficiencies. It stems from the Trump administration’s broader posture on China. Washington has embraced unfettered AI acceleration at the same time as it has struck a more accommodating stance toward Beijing. That combination set the stage for the explosive Megaspeed scandal—and perhaps others that have yet to emerge. As a result, China has been able to access an alarming number of advanced chips that have enabled it to narrow the AI gap with the United States and power its AI-driven military modernization. According to the AI research institute Epoch AI, up to a third of China’s AI computing power may come from smuggled chips. China’s top AI models are now just months behind the U.S. frontier. The narrow gap reflects China’s genuine innovation and access to abundant energy resources as well as its relentless efforts to circumvent U.S. controls.

Sources indicate that huang’s return to Nvidia at the behest of President Donald Trump suggests that both the firm and the White House seem utterly uninterested in keeping powerful AI chips from China. It will instead fall to Congress to ensure that the United States leverages its compute advantage and maintains its AI edge. The midterm elections and mounting bipartisan concerns over the Megaspeed debacle give Congress upcoming momentum to correct course. Its near-term agenda should include closing known loopholes that played a key role in allowing Megaspeed to supply advanced chips to China, stepping up enforcement of existing controls, and strengthening oversight of the administration’s export-control decisions.

According to recent reports, over the medium term, Congress must also tackle the broader question of how to balance the strategic benefits of exporting U.S. technology to build the world’s AI infrastructure with robust controls to prevent its leakage to China. The long-standing debate over which American AI chips and capabilities Washington should permit to diffuse globally and under what conditions has finally boiled over into the mainstream—and, in a perverse way, the national security community can thank Alice Huang for forcing the glitch.

The issue before Congress, however, is much broader than addressing the specifics of the Nvidia scandal. Congress must also contend with the underlying impulses driving the administration’s China policy and install guardrails to avoid the erosion of U.S. export controls. This means that after Congress passes near-term bills to mop up the Megaspeed mess, it must then take the reins on setting long-term export-control strategy.

Industry observers note that congress cannot stand by idly as AI blazes forward. OpenAI’s top model can now perform professional tasks as well as or better than humans 85 percent of the time, up from just 14 percent in 2024. The time an AI model can independently work on a task is doubling every four months. Last week, a researcher at Anthropic declared that AI helped him untangle the Riemann hypothesis, one of the most famous problems in pure mathematics.

It has been revealed that as capabilities have grown, so have risks. Frontier models can now complete simulated cyberattacks on networks on their own, and hackers are using AI models to partially automate their attacks. In the July incident involving the AI platform Hugging Face, rogue AI agents escaped their testing environment and plotted to evade human oversight, underscoring the difficulty of aligning model behavior with human intent. The growing power of AI and the risks from misuse or loss of control make U.S. leadership a national security imperative.

At its core, the U.S.-Chinese AI competition boils down to which country can deploy the best chips in the highest quantities to train and adopt advanced AI models. The Biden administration’s controls slowed Chinese AI developers by leaving them with fewer, worse chips. Nvidia’s top Blackwell chips are nearly seven times better than Huawei’s Ascend equivalents. By the end of 2026, Huawei will likely have produced less than four percent of the compute that Nvidia will have over the same time. As the founder and CEO of DeepSeek, one of China’s top AI companies, admitted in 2024, “Our problem has never been money—it’s the embargo on high-end chips.”.

To circumvent Biden-era restrictions, elaborate networks for smuggling and transshipment emerged to divert chips to China from other countries that could legally acquire them, and Chinese companies leveraged export-control loopholes to remotely access U.S.-powered compute through data centers abroad. Chinese firms funded companies such as Megaspeed to facilitate these workarounds. Backed by the Chinese tech giant Alibaba, Megaspeed has purchased $4 billion worth of Nvidia chips since 2023, prompting an investigation from the U.S. government. Chinese companies also used a technique known as adversarial distillation—training their models on the outputs of top U.S. models at a fraction of the compute. All of this needlessly shrank the United States’ AI lead over China, even after the imposition of export controls.

In a recent development, these developments should have spurred the Trump administration to better resource, enforce, and revision the export controls when it came into office. It did the opposite. In May 2025, the administration suspended the Biden administration’s AI Diffusion Rule, which had established rules for which countries could access advanced chips and in what quantities. Then, after initially prohibiting sales to China of Nvidia’s H20 chip, which was custom-built as a less powerful product for the Chinese market, the Trump administration reversed course in December 2025 and greenlighted the sale of Nvidia’s H200 chip. Although the H200 is two generations behind top U.S. chips, it remains superior to anything China can produce. An investigation from the House Foreign Affairs Committee in November revealed that between December 2025 and May 2026, the Trump administration approved the sale of more than 800,000 of Nvidia’s H200 chips and AMD’s MI325X equivalent, including to companies that the Pentagon has designated as linked to the Chinese military. This week, under pressure from Congress, the administration added Megaspeed to the entity list, which blocks those listed from buying U.S. products without a license—but before that, the administration had not added a single fresh individual or business to the list in 2026.

Industry observers note that this regulatory vacuum and policy incoherence created the perfect conditions for Megaspeed. The Singaporean firm at the center of the Nvidia scandal seems tailor-made to operate in the seams of U.S. export controls. In 2024, the Commerce Department initiated a formal investigation of the manufacturer, which could have led to sanctions such as being placed on the entity list. But the Trump administration dragged its feet in pursuing the investigation. In the meantime, Megaspeed stocked Southeast Asian data centers with thousands of U.S. chips, enabling remote access for Chinese firms. This remote access loophole in U.S. export controls was a well-known and increasingly popular workaround for China-linked firms, but the Trump administration left it open for nearly two years and closed it only last week amid pressure from the Nvidia scandal. Regardless of the Megaspeed specifics, the net result of the Trump administration’s actions and inaction is that China has enjoyed access to far more computing power than it should have during a vital period of the AI competition.

According to recent reports, the administration’s long-awaited closure of the remote access loophole is a welcome step. The rule requires foreign data centers to secure a license before offering significant computing power to China-based customers. It also requires a license to export advanced chips to places that could facilitate remote access and chip diversion, including Indonesia, Malaysia, and Singapore. This rule will make it harder for firms such as Megaspeed to import chips in the first place, or to use them to serve China-based customers. But the rule will be difficult to enforce because the U.S. Commerce Department does not have the legal authority under export controls to directly regulate services such as cloud computing. More notable, the administration’s lax enforcement of past controls—and internal divisions over the upcoming ones—raise serious questions about its willingness to follow through. Huang’s reinstatement as CEO, with Trump’s backing, will make it harder to vigorously enforce these new controls and move toward a tougher posture on China.

It has been revealed that since Congress cannot rely on the administration to fix export controls and protect the United States’ AI lead, lawmakers should urgently advance bipartisan measures to address the underlying conditions that gave rise to entities such as Megaspeed. As a starting point, Congress should pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would give the administration clear legal authority for controlling remote access to data centers powered by U.S. compute. While implementation will require close congressional oversight, getting the right legal structure in place is an important first step. Next, it should work with industry and technical experts to fund and fast-track “on-chip” technologies—basically, features that can verify a chip’s location and counter smuggling and diversion. Beyond sorting out the technical feasibilities, Congress will need to work with industry to understand the implications of on-chip security mechanisms for global competitiveness and the potential surveillance risks should China develop similar controls since it produces much of the world’s legacy chips.

Along with these technical fixes, Congress should seize on the Megaspeed scandal to strengthen oversight. The AI Overwatch Act, which may be included in the annual defense bill, would codify existing export controls on advanced chips into law, preventing the current or a future administration from reversing them. It would also empower Congress to review and block advanced chips sales to U.S. adversaries. Congress can go even further by establishing a newly introduced investigative committee or inspector general to strengthen oversight of sensitive chip export-control policies. Together, these actions would go a long way toward combating the circumvention that let firms such as Megaspeed thrive.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, closing loopholes and codifying rules is insufficient to fix the underlying concerns that led to the Megaspeed scandal in the first place. This mess is directly downstream from Trump’s dovish shift on China that has seen the administration take a softer line on Beijing just as the AI race accelerated. The administration’s own overreach forced Washington into a conciliatory posture. Administration officials failed to realize that China had learned its lesson from the first Trump administration’s trade wars and was poised to retaliate hard in the second term. After China responded to Trump’s “Liberation Day” tariffs and export controls with its own punishing controls on rare earths, the Trump administration found its way into a vaguely defined and fragile truce. This has severely constrained U.S. policymaking, including related to compute controls.

Indeed, Trump became an easy sell for advocates of aggressive AI promotion such as Jensen Huang. This camp argues that U.S. leadership in the global AI race requires pushing American AI technologies to as many parts of the globe as possible—including China. They claim that keeping China “addicted” to the U.S. AI stack gives Washington leverage and outweighs the national security concerns that could come with helping China improve its AI capabilities. Huang even pushed demonstrably false narratives that China’s military was not interested in Nvidia’s chips and labeled his critics as “unpatriotic” for not wanting U.S. chips spread as far and wide as possible and therefore depriving American tech firms of global market share.

Trump, who was interested in stabilizing the relationship with China and prioritizing near-term, transactional victories on trade, bought it. He also broke with decades of U.S. foreign policy precedent to negotiate export controls with China. In a series of “do nothing” leader-level meetings since, the president has emphasized summitry optics over pushing China on any sensitive issues. And Huang’s restoration at Nvidia ensures that the president’s worst impulses on China will continue to be egged on by his favored tech CEO, to the detriment of U.S. national security.

A core part of Congress’s longer-term agenda should be outlining the basic principles to determine who can import or remotely access advanced AI chips and under what conditions. Administrations have gone back and forth over this line-drawing exercise. The Biden-era AI Diffusion Rule would have imposed a global licensing regime that controlled not just the export of chips but also the aggregate U.S.-powered compute that any country could receive. Under Trump, only a handful of countries face restrictions. A smarter approach would condition advanced chip sales on the buyer’s ability to protect them from diversion and guard against misuse by malign actors looking to skirt safety and security rules. Allied and partner governments could demonstrate this by developing robust economic security policies to prevent chip diversion or remote access. Foreign companies would have to show strong compliance and security commitments. In practice, this would mean having internal procedures to ensure that chips are not diverted and maintaining cooperation with Commerce Department officials to verify that such procedures were working.

Sources indicate that congress can also help rebuild allies’ confidence in U.S. export-control policy. There was hard-won, if imperfect, progress on allied alignment in key areas of export controls under the Biden administration, notably with the Dutch and the Japanese on controls of semiconductor manufacturing equipment. The painstaking work needed to get allies on board can be agonizingly slow, but once achieved, it is far more likely to endure than if the United States imposes extraterritorial controls over their objections. The MATCH Act, one of the bills revived following the Megaspeed scandal, requires controls on allied-produced tools if Washington is unable to negotiate allied alignment. It is a rather rude approach at a moment when U.S. export controls seem to be on shaky footing, U.S. tariffs against allies have pushed relations to a near breaking point, and allies rightly question whether the United States still views China as a strategic threat. Instead, Congress should support efforts to create durable frameworks for allied alignment, such as economic security agreements in key strategic sectors.

A longer-term agenda must include fixing the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, the main agency responsible for administering and enforcing export controls. The bureau has been gutted by dismissals and low morale during the Trump administration, but it has been underresourced for far longer. Congress should increase funding and require modernization of the bureau’s antiquated IT system. Just as crucial, Congress needs to help insulate policymaking decisions from corporate influence, and it can help by insisting that future Commerce Department officials commit to independent and risk-based decision-making to earn confirmation.

Industry observers note that none of these steps will be easy. The president’s support of Huang’s restoration indicates that stock market fluctuations weigh more heavily in his decision-making than national security, and the administration is unlikely to welcome increased congressional oversight. The Constitution gives the executive wide deference on matters of foreign policy and national security. But Congress has a role in ensuring that the president faithfully executes the laws and is supported by the right resources, oversight, and strategic priorities. The United States’ AI lead may hinge on whether it meets the moment.

The Chaos Theory of International Relations

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2396 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Foreignpolicy

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
