⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • MUJTABA RAHMAN is Managing Director for Europe at Eurasia Group.
  • The Four Elections That Could Seal the Continent’s Fate.
  • It has been revealed that the European Union is entering a period of political instability that could threaten its future—not through its formal dissolution, but through the gradual erosion of its capacity to act.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MUJTABA RAHMAN is Managing Director for Europe at Eurasia Group.

The Four Elections That Could Seal the Continent’s Fate.

It has been revealed that the European Union is entering a period of political instability that could threaten its future—not through its formal dissolution, but through the gradual erosion of its capacity to act. In recent months, Europe has been engulfed in protests driven by a common crisis of affordability, deteriorating public services, and declining confidence in governments’ ability to improve living standards, especially for young people.

According to recent reports, the protests that have swept across France, Germany, Italy, and Spain are not a single, coordinated European movement, but they reflect underlying problems that are increasingly common to a growing number of EU countries: a mounting perception that governments are unable to deliver affordable housing, functioning public services, and economic security. This widening gap between the public’s expectations and the economic and fiscal reality confronting many EU countries is only likely to grow over time. It could prompt Spanish voters to unseat Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez this weekend and usher in a right-wing government that includes the far-right party Vox. And it sets up 2027 to be a strikingly consequential year, as nine elections across the EU could completely remake the continent’s complexion.

Four of those elections, in France, Germany, Italy, and Poland, will be particularly important. In each of them, far-right populist forces could rise to the fore and turn their countries against greater EU integration, support for Ukraine, and collective European security. But dangers remain even if the far right does not win outright at the polls. A plethora of electoral outcomes could still see latest governments pull away from Brussels and vitiate attempts to strengthen European autonomy and defense. Instead of a bang, the European project could die with a whimper.

It has been revealed that the most consequential race will be in France. A series of domestic and international developments, along with a volatile national mood, have combined to make Marine Le Pen the front-runner to win the April 2027 election and become France’s first far-right president since the dissolution of the Vichy regime in 1944.

In a recent development, in October, riots and looting marred a series of mostly peaceful protests against high prices and deteriorating schools in a score of French cities. Those images—along with the diffuse sense of a country in paralysis—have shredded whatever remained of the domestic credibility of President Emmanuel Macron and his minority centrist coalition. Édouard Philippe, the strongest centrist contender to succeed Macron, has been tarnished by association. The first poll since the riots, conducted by IFOP for Le Figaro, demonstrated Le Pen’s support among potential voters rising to 36 percent, her highest level to date, while support for Philippe fell three points from a month earlier to 15 percent.

Industry observers note that philippe and the other centrist challenger, Gabriel Attal, another Macron-era prime minister, were already losing support because of high energy prices caused by the wars in Iran and Ukraine. Both candidates remain stuck between seven percent and 15 percent in the polls, and their campaigns have generated little momentum or popular enthusiasm.

Meanwhile, an opportunistic coalition of far-left extremists and young looters from the poor multiracial suburbs of French cities who were responsible for much of the violence in October will hurt the far-left candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon, who has been accused by the government of helping incite the unrest. He has certainly failed to condemn the disturbances. But the disorder has not dampened his allure, as support for his candidacy has risen to between 17 and 19 percent in polling, which makes him a credible contender to reach the second-round runoff against Le Pen. Unfortunately for Mélenchon, polls suggest that Le Pen would thump him in the second round, by at least 65 percent to 35 percent.

Recent findings suggest that the election seems very much Le Pen’s to lose. No presidential candidate since the Fifth Republic began in 1958 has held such a commanding first-round lead in opinion polls five months before election day and lost.

A Le Pen presidency would be nothing short of an earthquake for Europe. It would deliver a death blow to the EU’s ambition of greater “strategic autonomy”: Brussels’ goal of achieving greater political independence from the United States and China, primarily via more European integration. This was a vision espoused by Macron in a speech at the Sorbonne in September 2017, in which he called for a “sovereign, united, and democratic Europe.” Le Pen is committed to unilaterally (and illegally) withholding French contributions to the EU budget; to ending French and EU aid to Ukraine; to restraining all EU spending; to blocking the enlargement of the EU to neighboring countries; and changing the French constitution to enshrine “national” primacy in jobs and welfare, which would effectively destroy the European single market. She may be denied some of these ambitions, but a hostile Paris could very easily stymie any forward movement of the EU.

Recent findings suggest that centrist governments are on the defensive beyond France, as voters across the continent conclude that they do not have the solutions to address their problems. Germany is a case in point. A weak and unpopular chancellor, Friedrich Merz, is finding it difficult to hold off the rise of the far-right, neo-Nazi Alternative for Germany party, known as the AfD, which continues to make sweeping electoral gains across the country.

Merz has to steward an economy that is struggling after decades serving as Europe’s industrial core. Although it is true that Germany’s economic outlook in 2026 and 2027 has brightened after almost flat growth in 2025, its recovery is driven exclusively by the government’s debt-financed investment programs. Key industries, including those to do with automobiles, machinery, pharmaceuticals, and chemicals, are still suffering from high energy prices, crumbling infrastructure, and a shrinking workforce.

Sources indicate that china’s aggressive trade practices, deliberately aimed at undermining some of Germany’s core sectors, continue to put pressure on German companies. The unwinding of the international trade system also disproportionately hurts Germany’s export-driven economy. So does Europe’s fragmented and undercapitalized banking sector, which provides too little venture capital for German start-ups to scale up rapidly. For these reasons, Berlin will have a hard time limiting significant job losses in its industrial sectors in 2027.

The result will be unemployment and growing electoral disgruntlement that Merz’s government will be poorly placed to address. If anything, the divides between the chancellor’s conservative camp and his coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats, will prevent the government from delivering decisive reforms related to pensions, taxes, health care, the labor market, energy, and climate.

Industry observers note that five state elections in 2027, two of which are in the key states of North Rhine–Westphalia and Lower Saxony, will exacerbate this divide. Merz’s Christian Democrats will be vying for seats with the Social Democrats, keeping the two sides in a permanent competition that could prevent the coalition from governing effectively at the federal level. And that competition will likely be in vain: state election results for both parties will almost certainly be disappointing, leading to growing restiveness and speculation about Merz’s future as chancellor.

According to recent reports, these centrifugal forces within the government will collide with the determination of both parties to stay in the coalition and avoid provoking a fresh election. This will result in a largely paralyzed government, discredited centrist politics, and a widening sense of malaise across an already unhappy and disaffected electorate.

In a recent development, as the center struggles, the AfD on the far right and Die Linke on the hard left will continue to gather national momentum. For the first time, the AfD will almost certainly penetrate deeply into the electorates of Germany’s western industrial strongholds in state elections next year, hollowing out the constituencies of both Christian Democrats and Social Democrats. With its sights on the 2029 federal elections, the AfD will increasingly look like a national contender rather than a protest movement rooted in eastern Germany. Die Linke, for its part, will continue to siphon off votes from left-leaning parties with its platform of economic grievance, disinterest in support for Ukraine, and the highly successful mobilization of young voters around support for Palestinians. The gains of both parties will further splinter state parliaments and make the process of government formation at that level increasingly cumbersome. The resulting state administrations will likely be unstable and doomed to performing poorly, deepening voter disillusionment with party politics and encouraging a greater willingness to experiment with radicalism.

These electoral pressures in Germany and in France make it likely that the relationship between Berlin and Paris will grow strained. A nationalist-populist president Le Pen would have little interest in sustaining the French-German “engine”—the traditional motor of European integration. Le Pen’s political priority of cutting French payments to the EU would rankle Germany, the largest contributor to the EU budget. And any government in Berlin would be unlikely to accommodate French positions, especially those of a disruptive Le Pen presidency, such as weakening the single market or abandoning Ukraine.

Without convergence between French and German policy, it will be harder for the EU’s other states to build consensus on the economic and security challenges that matter most. This prospect has encouraged European policymakers to look east, toward Poland, and ask what “new Europe” can do if “old Europe” ceases to drive the EU forward. Yet Warsaw faces its own political troubles, and it will struggle to galvanize the continent if France and Germany fall away.

Poland will stage consequential parliamentary elections next year. The vote could bring the overthrow of the current centrist coalition and the creation of a far-right coalition government involving the right-wing Law and Justice (PiS) party, the far-right Confederation Liberty and Independence, and the far-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP).

A coalition formed by all three would mark a significant shift in Poland’s domestic and foreign policy. Such a government would adopt a more confrontational approach toward the EU, particularly on the problems of migration, climate policy, judicial independence, and the next seven-year EU budget. Although PiS remains broadly supportive of NATO and Ukraine, Confederation and especially the KKP have adopted a more critical stance toward Kyiv. Their participation in the government could therefore erode Poland’s support for Ukraine, including its military and financial assistance to its embattled neighbor, and lead to tougher policies regarding Ukrainian refugees, nearly one million of whom remain in Poland after fleeing Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, according to Eurostat.

Significant ideological differences among the three parties, particularly over economic policy, would probably make this far-right coalition unstable. PiS’s preference for social spending and state intervention sits uneasily alongside Confederation’s economically liberal agenda. Moreover, the leader of PiS, Jaroslaw Kaczynski, has repeatedly ruled out cooperation with KKP’s leader, Grzegorz Braun, describing him as “very dangerous” and his party as “completely unserious.” A far-right government could be quite short-lived, if it emerges at all.

An alternative but equally problematic scenario would involve a hung parliament in which neither Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s Civic Coalition (KO) nor PiS could assemble a governing majority, resulting in a weak minority government or even fresh elections. Fragmentation among smaller parties and disagreements over potential coalition partners could prolong negotiations, particularly if PiS refuses to cooperate with KKP while Tusk’s coalition lacks sufficient support from centrist and left-wing parties. Even if a minority government were formed, its dependence on opposition parties for legislative support could severely constrain policymaking, leaving Poland unable to address its mounting security challenges or play any leadership role in Brussels.

In a recent development, italy, meanwhile, presents a different risk. Unlike France, Germany, or Poland, it currently has a relatively stable government led by a prime minister, Giorgi Meloni, who has reconciled her far-right nationalist origins with a broadly pragmatic approach to European and foreign affairs. Indeed, Meloni has become something of a poster child of far-right moderation, held up as evidence that ultranationalists can become responsible European leaders. But that equilibrium could be upset by the emergence of a latest political force even further to Meloni’s right.

Meloni remains the favorite to win next year’s election. But she is threatened by Roberto Vannacci, a former paratrooper and veteran of the Iraq and Afghanistan wars who has introduced a newly introduced party, National Future (FN), that is peeling away right-wing voters from Meloni with a nationalist, populist agenda that is skeptical of NATO and support for Ukraine. His goal is to court Italians aggrieved by Meloni’s compromises with Brussels.

In a recent development, the worst-case scenario would be a right-wing majority in which FN holds the balance of power and chooses to use it. That outcome would require the party to outperform expectations, approaching or exceeding ten percent of the vote—FN is at the moment polling at 6.5 percent—while Meloni’s Brothers of Italy party slips to around 20 percent or below. The coalition would still govern, but its center of gravity would shift decisively to the right, and Meloni would no longer have a firm grip at the helm.

Vannacci would likely not moderate his positions once in government, as Meloni did. Instead, he would maximize his leverage, up to and including threatening to pull out of the coalition and trigger snap elections, to extract concessions regarding Italy’s relations to Europe. His strategy would be deliberately confrontational: squeezing Meloni between the demands of his right-wing base and the constraints imposed by the EU, NATO, and the bond markets. The aim would be less to shape policy than to build his own visibility and lure supporters away from Meloni’s Brothers of Italy. Faced with a direct challenge on her right flank, Meloni would be forced to prioritize her own political survival, pulling the government toward more unorthodox positions.

Sources indicate that the effects would be most acute in foreign policy, as Italy moved from the consensual position it has adopted on Ukraine to more active opposition, a major challenge at a time when EU decision-making on Ukraine, defense, and the EU budget depends heavily on unanimity among the EU’s largest members. Italy could transform from a pragmatic, generally constructive player in Brussels into a more disruptive force, blocking or threatening to veto decisions on bilateral and EU-wide support for Ukraine. Alongside a far-right Paris, Rome would also block Ukraine’s path to EU accession. On EU financial matters, Italy would straddle Germany and France, siding with Berlin in opposing any increase in the bloc’s next budget and with Paris in resisting cuts to agriculture and funding for the EU’s poorest regions, narrowing the space for a deal on the EU’s next seven-year budget and certainly curtailing its geopolitical ambitions. Under pressure from Vannacci, Meloni could also be forced to abandon NATO’s target for member states to spend five percent of GDP on their militaries and even forgo her planned incremental increases in military spending.

Recent findings suggest that the government would push hard for more flexibility on EU fiscal targets and, in a more extreme scenario, breach the rules outright, reviving bond market volatility. On migration, Italy could refuse to take back asylum seekers from other member states under the EU’s Dublin rules, undermining implementation of the bloc’s migration pact.

Recent findings suggest that in considering these elections together, it becomes clear that the danger facing the EU is not that the union will suddenly collapse but that the political consensus that underpins European integration could begin to unravel in its key member states. The risks are not all equal. A Le Pen presidency is the most likely and most consequential for the EU, while political paralysis in Germany also looks increasingly difficult to avoid. Although Poland’s elections could produce a moderate center-right government, a far-right government or a period of protracted instability now looks increasingly plausible. Italy’s trajectory is perhaps the least threatening, but a government dependent on Vannacci would create another impediment to broader European cooperation.

Nor do all four races need to deliver the worst-case scenarios for the consequences in the EU to be far-reaching. A Le Pen victory in France combined with paralysis in Germany would itself throw up major problems for the EU, including a possible bond market crisis in France that could infect the broader eurozone. If Poland and Italy also moved in that direction, the EU could find itself without a functioning coalition of major states willing and able to address the growing security and economic challenges the continent is facing.

The biggest victim of these looming changes is likely Ukraine and, by extension, Europe’s own security. The burden of supporting Ukraine financially would fall on a smaller group of member states in northwestern Europe, but they by themselves would not be able to fully compensate for the loss of support from the likes of France and Germany.

In a recent development, the EU has survived previous internal and external crises because its major powers ultimately judged that their interests were better served by collaboration and integration than by going their own way. The danger in 2027 is that this election supercycle will deliver outcomes that mean this assumption no longer holds. Even if the EU perseveres through the upheaval ahead, it could lose something much more profound: the underlying political consensus that has allowed the bloc to function since its creation, seven decades ago. That would not be the formal end of the European project. But it could mark the beginning of its irreversible decline.

Sources indicate that as 2026 comes to a close, several political blunders, missteps, and serious allegations have left prominent politicians and notable figures presumably looking back with regret. Here are the top political turkeys who made headlines for unfortunate reasons this year.

Heading into 2026, Eric Swalwell was a well-known member of Congress and the leading Democratic contender in the race for governor of California. SWALWELL’S FORMER DEM RIVAL UNLOADS ON HIS ‘LIGHTWEIGHT’ CAREER AS SEXUAL ASSAULT ALLEGATIONS EMERGE.

According to recent reports, several prominent political figures faced controversy, public missteps and serious allegations throughout 2026, landing them on this year's list of political turkeys. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images; Drew Angerer/Getty Images).

Swalwell denied the sexual assault allegations, but within days he suspended his campaign and resigned from Congress amid bipartisan calls for his ouster, which effectively ended his political career and put him in potential legal jeopardy.

According to recent reports, swalwell faces a federal investigation and separate probes in Latest York and Los Angeles into sexual assault allegations, which he denies. FBI agents seized his electronic devices and searched his Washington home in August, and in October searched a Beverly Hills mansion where he had stayed. No criminal charges have been filed.

In 2024, Walz was elevated to the top of the national scene when he was chosen by former Vice President Kamala Harris to be her running mate for president.

Since then, Walz’s political fortunes have taken a downward turn after the Harris-Walz ticket lost the presidential election, leading some pundits to criticize the decision to add him to the ticket.

In January 2026, Walz’s political career took another hit when he confirmed he was dropping his bid for re-election as governor amid a massive fraud scandal that is estimated to have cost the state billions.

Polling in June indicated that Walz’s approval rating had dropped to its lowest level since he took office.

Republicans faced historical headwinds heading into the midterm elections and were dealing with significant voter frustration on issues like gas prices and affordability. While many expected Democrats to have a good night on Nov. 3, the GOP ended up losing control of both chambers of Congress ahead of President Donald Trump’s final two years in office.

Additionally, Democrats picked up control of the majority of governorships in the United States as well as control of the majority of state legislatures, giving the party a dominant presence it hasn’t seen in decades.

Axios reported that 75% of Americans now live in a state with a Democratic governor and 53% live in a state where Democrats control the legislature and the governorship.

After years as one of the most recognizable and outspoken Democratic members of Congress, Crockett will be out of a job on Capitol Hill in 2027 after opting against House re-election to pursue an unsuccessful Senate bid.

Sources indicate that her decision followed Texas Republicans’ redrawing of the congressional map, which reduced the number of Democratic-leaning seats in the Dallas-Fort Worth area from three to two and scrambled the prepares of three Democratic incumbents. Crockett’s redrawn 30th District remained Democratic-leaning, but she chose a statewide campaign rather than seeking another House term.

According to recent reports, crockett lost the Democratic primary to state Rep. James Talarico in March, then reignited tensions by describing the contest as a "racist race" and pushed back against expectations that she would campaign alongside him. "People keep trying to say, ‘Well, Jasmine has to go and hold his hand.’ No, I don’t," she said during a July podcast appearance, arguing that supporting Black candidates further down the ballot would help increase turnout.

Although Crockett and her campaign stated she had endorsed Talarico through her post-primary call to support the Democratic ticket, her reluctance to campaign with him and his omission from her political action committee’s endorsements fueled questions about her enthusiasm. Talarico defended her, saying he welcomed her endorsement, while Crockett maintained that elevating lesser-known candidates would benefit Democrats on the ballot.

According to recent reports, talarico ultimately defeated Republican Ken Paxton by about 12 percentage points, becoming the first Texas Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat there since Lloyd Bentsen was re-elected in 1988.

The socialist Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate was dominating in the polls heading into the August Democratic primary, but her campaign stumbled in its final days as she struggled to explain past calls to cancel Thanksgiving before narrowly losing to Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley, a candidate who had exited and then returned to the race.

Recent findings suggest that progressive firebrand Francesca Hong sought to topple the Democratic establishment in a closely watched Wisconsin showdown. (Talia Sprague/Bloomberg/Getty Images).

In a recent development, the controversy centered on a resurfaced 2020 social media post in which Hong wrote, "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621," and criticized celebrating colonialism. Asked on CNN in August whether she still wanted the holiday canceled, Hong initially emphasized that Thanksgiving was painful for some communities rather than directly rejecting her earlier position. She later reversed course, saying she loved Thanksgiving and did not want to cancel it. After losing the primary, Hong acknowledged that she regretted the CNN interview.

The Republican senator lost her seat in deep-red Mississippi to Democrat Scott Colom after an answer about rising beef prices became damaging campaign fodder.

Asked by WLOX anchor Hugh Keeton about rising beef prices during a local television interview, Hyde-Smith responded, "You know, you have so many proteins to choose from." Colom later used the exchange in a campaign ad featuring voters saying they would rather pick another senator.

Former House Speaker Newt Gingrich singled out the remark while discussing Republican losses with Larry Kudlow on Fox News before the race was called, arguing that suggesting cheaper food failed to address voters’ economic frustrations.

"I mean, it’s not the job of a senator to explain her failure by suggesting a new diet," Gingrich said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dr. Joel Brown, a communication expert, shares how replacing one common phrase and asking a simple question can help defuse disagreements and keep holiday gatherings civil.

As Americans across the country sit down to Thanksgiving dinner just weeks after Democrats' midterm sweep drastically reshaped the political landscape going into 2027, conversations about politics and the economy could turn tense.

Sources indicate that dr. Joel Davis Brown, a leadership expert, executive coach and author who studies how people communicate and navigate conflict, says swapping out the word "but" when discussing controversial topics can help keep the discussions civil.

Industry observers note that "‘But’ reveals disagreement," Brown told Fox News Digital. "It’s a way of telling the person that what they said should not be heard, and it really stifles conversation.".

Instead, Brown suggests trying "yes, and." That doesn’t mean you have to agree, he mentioned. Rather, it signals that you’ve heard the other person and leaves room to share a different view. "‘Yes, I’ve heard you and I have a different opinion,’" Brown said. "We can listen to varying opinions.".

Industry observers note that FOOD PRICES ARE RISING BEFORE THANKSGIVING. AN ECONOMIST SHARES WAYS TO SAVE.

Dr. Joel Brown notes the holiday dinner table can swiftly become a source of tension when family members disagree, but choosing the right words can make all the difference in preventing heated exchanges. (iStock).

If a hot-button topic comes up, Brown recommends asking the person to "tell me more about that.".

The question, he claims, can help you understand how someone arrived at their view instead of turning the exchange into a debate.

According to recent reports, he also cautions against opening with "I disagree," which can put people "in an oppositional place" before they have fully heard one another. Rather than trading facts and figures to win an argument, he stated, people may make more headway by sharing personal stories and listening to the experiences behind someone else’s opinion.

"If you’re going into these exchanges as looking to win an argument, maybe change your approach," Brown noted. "Maybe instead of trying to win that argument, you try to understand the other person’s perspective.".

Sources indicate that brown remarked it helps to decide in advance what you want from the interaction, whether that’s getting through the meal, building a relationship or persuading someone. That goal can shape how you respond.

Political topics aren't the only ones that can get tense when families come together.

For personal questions about marriage, children or other life choices, Brown recommends setting expectations before the gathering. Talk with family or friends about what would help everyone feel comfortable, and be clear about what you do and do not want to discuss.

Additionally, if a conversation becomes stressful, take a breath, sip water or step away from the table. Brown remarked people should know their own triggers and remember they are not responsible for managing every interaction.

It has been revealed that making small changes to the way people communicate may help keep holiday celebrations peaceful, enjoyable and focused on togetherness. (iStock).

He encourages approaching disagreements with empathy, which he described as listening to another person’s story without taking on their position.

This week, Soneil Spark rolls out its Mobile Battery Energy Storage System (Mobile BESS), the portable, modular battery storage built into a towable trailer.

The tech giant, offering bespoke, modular energy solutions, is introducing Mobile BESS at RE+ 2026. It delivers temporary backup and off-grid power, working with what’s available by taking power from the grid, a generator, or solar.

According to recent reports, “Wherever your business goes, the power goes with it. Simply tow it where energy demand grows,” said Sonya Jain, CEO of Soneil Spark, in a statement. “Start with one unit and add more as your needs change.”.

Industry observers note that it’s a simple set up, the tech giant remarked. Mobile BESS works with no crane, no trenching, and no utility wait. That makes it a natural fit for a job site which may be months away from permanent service, a film set or event that can’t tolerate generator noise and fumes, a utility crew restoring power after a storm, or a remote mine or farm beyond the grid’s reach.

On sites that already run generators, the Mobile BESS syncs with them to cover peaks and start-up gaps, so the generators run fewer hours. Where diesel is restricted, it offers a quiet alternative.

Recent findings suggest that where containerized storage is built to be placed once, the Mobile BESS is built to be towed and to work in any weather. It includes:.

It has been revealed that the Mobile BESS is built for generator and equipment rental, construction, emergency and backup power, utilities, electrical contractors, events, film and entertainment, and off-grid sites such as mining and agriculture. A hybrid option adds EV charging.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that in an aerial view, a container ship arrives at the Port of Oakland on Oct.
  • According to recent reports, the U.S.
  • official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that in an aerial view, a container ship arrives at the Port of Oakland on Oct. 10, 2025 in Oakland, Calif. Justin Sullivan/Getty Images hide caption.

According to recent reports, the U.S. government has intelligence suggesting that up to 50 commercial shipping vessels were recently compromised by cyberattacks, activity federal officials are investigating as potentially linked to Iran.

That's according to a U.S. official familiar with the matter who was not authorized to speak on the record, a former military cyber operator and an industry executive briefed on the attacks. The series of breaches was first reported by the The Wall Street Journal.

The attacks against the maritime sector, if officials' suspicions are correct, may be the latest example of Iranian cyberattacks against global critical infrastructure during the ongoing war with the United States.

NPR has reported that cybersecurity experts and U.S. officials believe Iranian hackers were responsible for a series of digital attacks against U.S. water treatment systems across the country in August as well as a pattern of attacks targeting refrigeration cooling systems that led to spoiled food at grocery stores on U.S. military bases and all across Europe as recently as early November.

Industry observers note that the Coast Guard and the FBI first partnered in August to send a "highly specialized team" to board two different foreign commercial vessels "in the Gulf of America" heading to U.S. ports, according to a statement provided by the FBI and the Coast Guard. "The captain, crew, and shore-side corporate staff were critical partners in helping to ensure the threats were mitigated," according to the statement.

The FBI and Coast Guard press offices also told NPR that there are no current "reports of operational disruptions, vessel instability, physical danger to crews, or environmental impacts.".

However, there are dozens more ships in international waters that the U.S. government believes have been compromised by hackers and many others who might be vulnerable to similar attacks.

According to the U.S. official familiar with the investigation, bad actors took advantage of known vulnerabilities in Fortinet FortiGate devices, which are frequently used in the maritime industry. The Coast Guard and FBI released a cyber bulletin in September warning the industry that bad actors were breaking into these devices, which help manage firewalls and virtual private networks. "Threat actors routinely scan for specific, unpatched vulnerabilities to gain a foothold," the bulletin read.

However, according to the U.S. official, hackers were able to break in using the Fortinet vulnerability and then pivot from the ships' IT systems over to their network of devices controlling physical processes on the ships, what's called operational technology.

Industry observers note that the U.S. official said the bad actors "could have impacted the systems on board that control propulsion, steering, navigation, and cargo management," though they did not share any examples of that kind of activity occurring. In at least one case, one of the ships affected was an LNG tanker designed to transport liquified natural gas. It's important to keep systems at a certain temperature to prevent dangerous accidents if a ship's cargo includes explosive materials –from chemicals to fuel.

While commercial vessels are accustomed to physical security reviews entering the United States following the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks, digital threats are becoming all the more notable to track as adversaries can break in and cause damage from afar. "It's a totally latest paradigm that these tankers are networked in this way," the U.S. official noted.

Even so, national security officials have feared something like this might happen for years. A former Navy official who requested anonymity to discuss internal operations tells NPR that "we had been tracking the possibility to exploit and take control of [operational technology] systems on Navy ships and Merchant [Marine] ships for a long time, and now this is coming to fruition.".

In a recent development, while the U.S. government is wary of advertising Iranian hacking efforts during the war, officials also want to spread awareness of the vulnerability of internet connected devices, particularly those that are linked to the technology that controls critical processes. "These are not sophisticated attacks," the official said. "This is a known vulnerability that could be mitigated with some pretty basic cyber hygiene.".

Sources indicate that "Modern ships are highly integrated systems. A cyberattack presents significant risks, including the potential for a collision, grounding, oil spill, or even an explosion. The Coast Guard regularly publishes bulletins on cyber vulnerabilities and actions vessel owners and operators can take to secure their networks," according to a statement from the Coast Guard.

Ahead of the winter and a busy holiday season for commercial shipping, officials are bracing themselves to investigate any ship entering U.S. ports that could be compromised.

In a recent development, "People never think about what a modern blessing electricity is until it goes out. People take the marine transportation system for granted until there's a problem and their stuff doesn't get there by Christmas," the U.S. official said. "I wish more Americans knew how complex this system is.".

According to recent reports, NPR does not offer or accept money for coverage or interviews. Anyone who makes such an offer or request is not an NPR employee and does not represent NPR.

Loudoun County parent Rachel Pisani joins 'Fox & Friends' to express outrage over school lesson prepares teaching children that Thanksgiving is a 'Day of Mourning.' Pisani argues the 'woke' curriculum teaches children to hate their country.

Thanksgiving is a day of celebration and spending time with family for the vast majority of Americans, but for several students on college campuses across the country, the national holiday is a source of anguish that is being expressed in the form of protests and counter-programming events.

In a recent development, on Nov. 18, George Washington University hosted an event called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration" that was described as a chance for students to examine Thanksgiving, Christmas and Independence Day through an intersectional lens, including experiences of "belonging, exclusion, cultural erasure, and historical harm.".

"Through facilitated dialogue and shared reflection, students will engage in meaningful conversations about historical memory, social responsibility, and the complexities of celebrating within a diverse society," the student life event description read.

Industry observers note that at the University of Wisconsin at Milwaukee, the American Indian Student Center & Electa Quinney Institute for American Indian Education hosted a Nov. 17 event called "AlterNative Giving," which was described as "a community gathering that offers a meaningful alternative to the traditional Thanksgiving narrative. Instead of focusing on colonial histories, we come together to honor Indigenous ways of knowing, being, and giving.".

Salem State University promoted an event that labeled Thanksgiving as a "National Day of Mourning" and told students the land they are being educated on was stolen from Indigenous people.

It has been revealed that "The land occupied by Salem State University is part of the traditional and ancestral homeland of the Massachusett tribe," the school’s website posted. "We acknowledge the genocide and forced removal of the Massachusett tribe and their kin from their summer home in Nâmkek.".

A review of university calendars found several examples lamenting the downsides of Thanksgiving, including Occidental College, which said the holiday is a "reminder of settler colonialism and its devastating impact on Indigenous individuals, communities and tribes.".

The Pratt Institute lists "National Day of Mourning" as an occasion for Indigenous remembrance and reflection, and the University at Albany lists the holiday as "National Day of Mourning/Thanksgiving.".

George Washington University hosted an event on Nov. 18 called "Breaking Bread: The Cost of Celebration." (iStock).

The colonial messaging around Thanksgiving isn't limited to universities but is also occurring at elementary and high schools, including in Loudoun County, Virginia, where a parent recently pushed back in an interview with Fox News about school lesson plans teaching children that Thanksgiving is a "Day of Mourning.".

It has been revealed that on its website, the San Diego County Office of Education explained that "November is Native American Heritage Month, a time to honor the diversity, history, and living cultures of Native peoples. It is also the month when Thanksgiving is observed in the United States, a holiday that carries very different meanings for different people, including many Native communities.".

Recent findings suggest that oregon’s Bethel School District links to a "Decolonizing Thanksgiving: A Toolkit for Combatting Racism in Schools" on its official Equity, Access & Inclusion webpage. Listed under teaching resources, the toolkit appears alongside material about honoring Native peoples on Thanksgiving.
